Paramount's Movie Promise Is Worth Half the Job-Years Its California Exit Would Cost
A leaked L.A. County report puts Paramount's California exit at 2,750 to 5,550 job-years through 2031, against 1,020 to 2,760 job-years from its 30-films-a-year pledge.
The L.A. County Economic Development Corporation's September 10 document, first reported by Politico, estimates that relocating Paramount's headquarters and operations out of California costs the state 2,750 to 5,550 job-years and $1.01 billion to $2.03 billion in output between October 1, 2026 and September 30, 2031. A completed move costs 28,990 to 57,980 permanent full-time jobs and $10.6 billion to $21.2 billion annually. Paramount's post-merger commitment of 30 features a year for three years generates 1,020 to 2,760 job-years over the same window. Paramount filed its answer to the state antitrust complaint on September 11.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Paramount's 30-films-a-year pledge is a merger argument as much as a slate, and what binds a filmmaker is the minimum-picture guarantee written into their own deal.
The Facts
  • L.A. County Economic Development Corporation document dated September 10, 2026, leaked and first reported by Politico. Four pages.
  • Partial relocation, October 1, 2026 to September 30, 2031: loss of 2,750 to 5,550 job-years in California across all industries; $1.01 billion to $2.03 billion in lost economic output.
  • Completed relocation: permanent loss of 28,990 to 57,980 full-time jobs statewide; $10.6 billion to $21.2 billion in lost annual output. The report notes these are "more appropriately expressed as full-time jobs instead of job-years" because the employment is lost permanently.
  • Paramount's post-merger production commitment of 30 features a year for three years: 1,020 to 2,760 job-years and $377.7 million to $1.01 billion in output over the same October 2026 to September 2031 window.
  • Los Angeles has lost nearly 50,000 jobs and scores of productions over the past six years.
  • October 1 is the date Paramount begins paying $7 million a day to WBD shareholders if the deal fails, which Paramount has called "extraordinary losses" and which totals more than $635 million a quarter.
  • Paramount is seeking a $1.88 billion bond from the state plaintiffs and the WGA. Bond hearing September 24.
  • Paramount's September 11 Defendants' Answer to Complaint and Defenses, 25 pages, led by Beth Wilkinson: the antitrust suit "amounts to a series of attempted shortcuts and assumptions that collapse under scrutiny," and "Paramount's proposed merger with Warner Bros. (the 'Merger') will enhance competition, not diminish it."
  • AGs' antitrust action filed July 13, 2026. Trial set for March 2, 2027. Coalition led by California AG Rob Bonta and New York AG Letitia James.
  • Ellison has been reported as contemplating a move to Tennessee, Georgia or Texas. L.A. County Board of Supervisors voted unanimously in July to support the AGs' lawsuit.
  • Merger value: $111 billion.

An R-Rated Original Just Beat Universal's Entire Franchise Library
The Odyssey reaches $1.684 billion worldwide by Sunday, passing Jurassic World's $1.677 billion, on a 6.39x multiple and a 9 percent domestic drop in its eighth weekend.
Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey becomes Universal's highest-grossing release ever this weekend at $1.684 billion worldwide, ahead of 2015's Jurassic World at $1.677 billion, with $601.2 million domestic and $1.083 billion international. It is the highest-grossing R-rated film ever, past Deadpool & Wolverine's $1.33 billion, the third-biggest non-franchise title of all time, and the first non-sequel and non-remake to gross over $1 billion internationally since 2009. A 6.39x global multiple and a 9 percent eighth-weekend domestic drop returned it to No. 1 worldwide. Universal leads all studios at $4.92 billion this year.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Nolan took an R rating, no existing franchise and a format almost nobody books, and returned $1.684 billion, which is now the comparable a director brings into a first-dollar-gross conversation.
The Facts
  • Worldwide by Sunday: $1.684 billion. Passes Universal's prior record holder, 2015's Jurassic World, at $1.677 billion.
  • Split: $601.2 million domestic, $1.083 billion international.
  • 12th highest-grossing film ever; third-biggest non-franchise title of all time.
  • Global multiple: 6.39x. Returned to No. 1 worldwide in its eighth weekend, down only 9 percent domestically.
  • Highest-grossing R-rated film of all time, past Deadpool & Wolverine's $1.33 billion.
  • First non-sequel and non-remake to gross over $1 billion internationally since 2009.
  • Highest-grossing film ever for Imax at $486 million-plus worldwide.
  • Biggest opening for Nolan internationally and globally: $139.6 million international, $264.1 million worldwide.
  • Biggest Imax 70mm opening weekend domestically: $6.3 million. Biggest Universal R-rated opening weekend domestically: $123.5 million.
  • Nolan's highest-grossing film domestically, internationally and globally, past The Dark Knight's $534.9 million domestic.
  • Highest-grossing Universal Pictures release ever in 45 international markets including Australia, France, Italy, India and Korea. Second-highest-grossing Universal release domestically behind Jurassic World's $653.4 million.
  • Second-highest-grossing film of the year behind Sony's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, approaching $935 million-plus domestic by Sunday.
  • Universal leads all major studios at more than $4.92 billion to date this year; first to cross $4 billion globally and $3 billion internationally in 2026.
  • Donna Langley, Chairman of NBCUniversal Entertainment: "What Chris and Emma [Thomas] have created will go down as one of the most ambitious and brilliantly executed films in cinematic history. A generational event that galvanizes moviegoing itself."

Studios Stopped Developing and the Ideas Moved Outside
CAA's Roeg Sutherland told TIFF's new market that studios have stopped developing the way they used to and that the ideas directors and actors want are not coming through traditional routes.
At TIFF: The Market, CAA Co-Head of Media Finance Roeg Sutherland said studio development has contracted and that talent is hunting material outside the usual pipeline: "All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes." He said the market now resets every two weeks rather than every six months. FilmNation CEO Glen Basner said independent distributors package to reduce risk by pre-selling to streamers, which builds films for streaming rather than a theatrical proposition.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): When studios stop developing, the person holding the underlying material sets the terms of the package, and the option and the attachment now carry the leverage the development deal used to.
The Facts
  • Panel at TIFF: The Market, the Toronto International Film Festival's new film and TV market, with TIFF's Geoff Macnaughton.
  • Roeg Sutherland, Co-Head of Media Finance, CAA: "It's cyclical, [but] what is happening now is that things are changing so much quicker than they ever have. Instead of having to reset yourself every six months, you have to reset yourself every two weeks."
  • Sutherland: "Things will be uncomfortable, but we work in independent film; everything's uncomfortable pretty much all the time."
  • Sutherland: "Studios are not developing the way they used to, which presents an unbelievable opportunity to the independent community. All our talent, be they directors or actors, are desperately looking for great ideas. And those great ideas, for the most part, are not coming out of the traditional routes."
  • Glen Basner, CEO, FilmNation Entertainment, on independent distributors: "This is my biggest complaint about the independent distribution community right now. There's a very traditional approach to packaging. They're worried about how much risk they're taking, and so they know they need to mitigate that by selling their movie to pay television, and specifically to streamers. The only problem is that we're [then] building movies for the streamer companies. That may work great on streaming, but it's not the same thing as building a theatrical proposition."
  • Basner: "We are trying to evolve to say, 'how do we make the best possible film so that it can compel people, in an undeniable way, to see it in a movie theater?' And if they do go and see it, then it's going to work in home video, it's going to work on pay TV, it's going to work on free television."
  • Basner on theatrical: "I think 2027 is going to be a great year at the theatrical box office."

Amazon Canceled an Emmy Winner Over Cost, Then Went Back for Four More Spider-Man Scripts
Prime Video canceled Spider-Noir days before it won five Creative Arts Emmys, and Sony TV and Prime are now weighing four new Spider-Man universe scripts, with one or two possibly moving forward.
The Ankler reports that Sony TV under Katherine Pope and Prime Video are weighing four Spider-Man universe scripts, from Kelvin Yu, Alison Tatlock, Ben H. Winters, and the team of Ben Nedivi, Matt Wolpert and Megan McDonnell, with Prime potentially ordering one or two. Spider-Noir was canceled days before winning five Creative Arts Emmys, and sources attribute the cancellation to its cost. Marvel reversed a second season of Wonder Man after Yahya Abdul-Mateen II earned a comedy actor nomination. HBO's Lanterns drew 10 million global viewers on August 30 and still has no renewal.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Five Creative Arts Emmys did not save Spider-Noir and a nomination did not save Wonder Man, so the protection that matters in a series deal is the episodic cost ceiling and a guaranteed second-season order.
The Facts
  • Prime Video canceled Spider-Noir days before the show won five Creative Arts Emmys, including Darran Tiernan's cinematography award. Sources say the show "ultimately fell victim to its price tag." Reps for Amazon and Sony TV declined to comment.
  • Sony TV (president Katherine Pope) and Prime Video are weighing four Spider-Man universe scripts. Prime may move forward with one or two. Loglines under wraps.
  • The four projects: Kelvin Yu (American Born Chinese); Alison Tatlock (Pluribus); Ben H. Winters (Tracker, Legion); and the duo of Ben Nedivi and Matt Wolpert (For All Mankind, Umbrella Academy) with Megan McDonnell (WandaVision, Agatha All Along, The Marvels).
  • Spider-Noir was the first Sony TV Marvel-universe show to reach air. Conceived in 2019 as part of a larger universe under Phil Lord and Chris Miller. The first series, Silk: Spider Society, was killed in 2024 after more than two years in development under showrunner Angela Kang.
  • Spider-Noir was a Nicolas Cage vehicle, presented in both color and black and white, with strong reviews but less staying power than lower-cost Prime originals Off Campus and Reacher.
  • Marvel reversed course on a second season of Wonder Man; star Yahya Abdul-Mateen II was nominated for best actor in a comedy series.
  • Marvel's remaining live-action TV slate at Disney: VisionQuest (Disney+, October 14) and Daredevil: Born Again season three (March).
  • HBO's Lanterns, from showrunner Chris Mundy, drew 10 million global viewers for its August 30 episode and is the highest-rated DC series on HBO Max; renewal is not imminent. A season two writers room opened ahead of the August 16 debut, with Chris Cantwell installed as co-showrunner in May after Damon Lindelof and Tom King departed.
  • DC's remaining live-action TV slate: The People v. Gorilla Grodd, greenlit August 21.
  • Starz sets the third and final season of P-Valley, from creator Katori Hall, for December 4, four years after the prior season.
  • An unnamed lit agent: "There's still a huge appetite for superhero shows; nobody can deny their power when they're done right... When Wonder Man gets canceled, it's about the [viewership] numbers and budget, and superhero shows are at the higher end of the budget spectrum."

The NFL Took Equity in a Studio and Routes Its Movies Through One Company
Hallmark's third NFL holiday movie premieres October 17; the first drew 3.7 million viewers as 2024's most-watched cable movie, and the NFL holds equity in Paramount Skydance.
Hallmark's Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story, made with the NFL and Skydance Sports, opens Hallmark's holiday slate on October 17. The 2024 Chiefs film was the most-watched cable movie of that year at 3.7 million viewers; the Bills sequel drew 2.3 million. Skydance Sports formed in 2022 as a joint venture with the league, and the NFL took equity in the combined company after the Skydance-Paramount merger. Skydance Sports head Jason Reed calls his team the league's "production and creative conduit," overseeing Dan Fogelman's Hulu series The Land and David O. Russell's Nicolas Cage feature for Prime Video.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): The NFL's longform output runs through one production conduit the league partly owns, so access to its teams, stadiums and marks is a relationship term rather than a license anyone can buy.
The Facts
  • Holiday Touchdown: A Bears Love Story is the third film in the Hallmark, NFL and Skydance Sports partnership. It opens Hallmark's holiday lineup on October 17.
  • Holiday Touchdown: A Chiefs Love Story (2024) was the most-watched cable movie of 2024 with 3.7 million total viewers. The Buffalo Bills sequel drew 2.3 million.
  • The NFL reports about 250 million fans in the United States, almost half of them women.
  • Skydance Sports was formed in 2022 as a joint venture with the NFL. After the Skydance-Paramount merger last year the NFL took equity in the combined company; Jason Reed says his team remains the league's "production and creative conduit."
  • Skydance Sports also oversees Dan Fogelman's upcoming Hulu series The Land, centered on a fictionalized Cleveland Browns, and David O. Russell's Prime Video feature starring Nicolas Cage as John Madden.
  • Hallmark declined to discuss the deal structure. Hallmark Media president Darren Abbott says it is part of a new "One Hallmark" initiative integrating entertainment, retail, and a division running cruises, pop-ups and touring live shows. Hallmark makes and sells licensed NFL product through 1,100 specialty stores and mass retailers.
  • Hallmark makes nearly 100 original movies and series a year, about a third in the holiday lineup. Some begin development two years out; the Bears movie locked its partner, prepped, filmed and premieres inside five months, on a 16-day shoot.
  • Cast: Lyndsy Fonseca, Robert Buckley, Marsha Mason, Khary Payton, with cameos from Bears head coach Ben Johnson, current players and alumni, and mascot Staley Da Bear.
  • Reed: "There are 250 million self-reported fans of the NFL in the United States, which basically means almost everybody... We thought that there was an opportunity to both provide content that would service that audience but also bring fans who don't yet know they're fans into the tent."
  • Origin: during the 2023-24 postseason the Chiefs posted a spoof trailer for a Hallmark-style movie called Falling for Football; Kansas City-based Hallmark set a meeting and fast-tracked a real film for that holiday season.

A Director's Format Choice Is Now Driving Imax's Capital Plan
Imax's CFO told investors The Odyssey's $457 million on Imax screens has opened exhibitor talks about second screens and higher capacity, with Dune: Part Three selling 70mm tickets four months early.
At the Goldman Sachs Communacopia and Technology Conference, Imax CFO Natasha Fernandes said The Odyssey, shot entirely on Imax cameras, has grossed $457 million on Imax screens globally and $66 million on Imax 70mm, making it the highest-grossing Imax release ever. She called the film a "proof point" that has opened deals with international exhibitors for second screens and higher-capacity sites. CMO Anne Globe said Dune: Part Three going to Imax 70mm allowed ticket sales four months ahead of the wide rollout, as happened on The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day. Imax shares rose in May on sale speculation.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Nolan's decision to shoot the whole film on Imax cameras is moving an exhibitor's capital spending and its advance on-sale window, which makes format commitment a term a director can trade rather than a preference.
The Facts
  • Imax CFO Natasha Fernandes and CMO Anne Globe spoke at the Goldman Sachs Communacopia + Technology Conference on Wednesday, September 9.
  • The Odyssey has grossed $1.6 billion in theaters and $457 million across Imax screens globally to date, the highest-grossing Imax release of all time. It was shot entirely with Imax cameras.
  • Imax 70mm screenings of The Odyssey have earned a cumulative $66 million worldwide; the company has added dates in Nolan's preferred format.
  • Fernandes: "I'm sure they've taken note of how The Odyssey was released, and how Nolan graciously leaned into Imax." She called the film a "proof point about our business and about the future of our business."
  • Fernandes on exhibitor demand: "There's many deals coming into play right now, like opportunities for second screens or higher capacity."
  • Imax also played Marvel-Sony's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, at $1.55 billion to date.
  • Globe said Dune: Part Three heading to Imax 70mm allowed early ticket sales four months in advance of the wider theatrical rollout, as with The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day.
  • Globe: "We're seeing that brand growth and we're seeing our fan base expand and continue to be excited about what's being offered in Imax."
  • Imax's share price rose in May 2026 amid Wall Street chatter about a sale and early-stage talks with possible suitors. Fernandes: "We occupy a unique position in the entertainment industry. We're connected with filmmakers and studios, and we have a global reach. So I think we're definitely a highly valued asset."

Microsoft Is Opening Blizzard's Game Library to Outside Screen Partners
Blizzard president Johanna Faries announced a Diablo animated series in development at Netflix at BlizzCon, with Blizzard saying it is "only the beginning, with even more taking shape across our universes."
Blizzard president Johanna Faries announced at the BlizzCon 2026 opening ceremony in Anaheim that an animated Diablo series is in development at Netflix. Blizzard's statement said the company is "partnering with some creative powerhouses to tell even more stories beyond gaming across new screens" and that "this is only the beginning, with even more taking shape across our universes." Diablo launched in 1996 and marks its 30th anniversary this year; Diablo IV shipped in 2023. This is the first BlizzCon since Microsoft closed its $69 billion Activision Blizzard acquisition in 2023.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Blizzard is licensing its universes out rather than building a studio around them, so the writers and producers who adapt them work against a publisher's rights, and sequel and spinoff participation is the term that decides whether the work compounds.
The Facts
  • An animated TV series adaptation of Diablo is in development at Netflix. No further details released.
  • Announced by Blizzard president Johanna Faries during the opening ceremony of BlizzCon 2026 at the Anaheim Convention Center on Saturday, September 12. The two-day fan festival runs September 12-13.
  • Blizzard's official description: "After decades of bringing entire universes to life through our games, we're partnering with some creative powerhouses to tell even more stories beyond gaming across new screens. A new animated series set in the world of 'Diablo' is in development with Netflix. More details will be shared in the future, but this is only the beginning, with even more taking shape across our universes."
  • Diablo is set in Sanctuary, where humanity is caught between the High Heavens and the Burning Hells. The first game launched in 1996, making 2026 the franchise's 30th anniversary. Diablo IV launched in 2023.
  • This is the first BlizzCon since Microsoft closed its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard in 2023.
  • Faries: "BlizzCon in and of itself represents so much for all of us to be able to shine a light on all the great work going on at Blizzard. We have put a lot of thought into this moment, and why now, and how do we continue to capture and build on the momentum we're experiencing as an organization."
  • Blizzard's other universes named in coverage of the event: World of Warcraft and Overwatch. StarCraft 3, an open-world shooter, was announced for 2030.

Searchlight Says Its New Filmmakers Now Come From YouTube
Searchlight president Matthew Greenfield told TIFF's market that YouTube lets filmmakers build audiences without gatekeepers, and that the studio finds material there it would not see through short films or first features.
At TIFF: The Market, during a live recording of The Town, Searchlight president Matthew Greenfield said YouTube has become a primary source of new storytellers. "It used to be that we would find, collectively in the industry, new talent from short films, from first features, from short stories. But all of those had to go through gatekeepers in one form or another," he said. "With YouTube, obviously, people can go direct and find and build their own audience." Studios have been scouring the platform since Obsession and Backrooms.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A filmmaker who built the audience on YouTube arrives holding the thing the studio used to be the only source of, which changes what a first deal has to concede on rights retention and sequel control.
The Facts
  • Matthew Greenfield, president of Searchlight Pictures, spoke at TIFF: The Market, the Toronto International Film Festival's new film and TV market, during a live recording of the industry podcast The Town.
  • Greenfield: "YouTube is an incredible resource, and we're always looking for new storytellers."
  • Greenfield: "One of the things that's super exciting about [YouTube] is that it used to be that we would find, collectively in the industry, new talent from short films, from first features, from short stories. But all of those had to go through gatekeepers in one form or another. With YouTube, obviously, people can go direct and find and build their own audience. And we can find things that wouldn't have come through the standard [avenues]. So, for sure, it's an exciting place to find new talent."
  • Deadline notes that after Obsession and Backrooms, studios and producers are scouring YouTube for the next big property originating on the platform.
  • Greenfield on theatrical: "Familiarity is the challenge that we have to battle against. How do we tell stories that feel new, that feel fresh, that feel interesting, that feel worthy of a theatrical experience?"
  • Greenfield: "Everybody has to decide every time they go to a movie: should I pay X dollars, make a real effort, get out of the house, travel, pay to see a movie in the theater, which is a great experience if you're seeing something you love. Or, should I stay at home and watch everything that has ever been made in the history of human culture?"

Creators Are Selling Tools Around the Archive, Not Just the Newsletter
Two former Substack executives launched a consultancy arguing subscriptions are no longer enough, pointing to Lenny Rachitsky's $400-a-year tier bundling more than $30,000 of software discounts.
Puck reports that former Substack executives Austin Tedesco and Catherine Valentine have launched a consultancy, Spur, arguing that creator businesses need products beyond newsletters, podcasts and events as AI aggregation erodes search and social traffic. Tedesco said AI now makes personalized tools cheap enough for creators to build against their own archives. Lenny Rachitsky's Product Pass bundles roughly 25 software tools he valued at $25,000 in January and more than $30,000 now, for a tier costing $400 a year; his newsletter has about 1.2 million total subscribers. Patreon found 81 percent of creators want a direct channel to fans.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): The money here sits with whoever owns the direct relationship to the audience, because the products are built against the archive and the subscriber list, and both are assets a distribution deal can quietly take.
The Facts
  • Austin Tedesco and Catherine Valentine, two former Substack executives, are launching a consultancy called Spur. The news was broken by Emily Sundberg's Feed Me.
  • Their thesis: as AI threatens web traffic, creator businesses need higher-value membership perks beyond dinners, conferences or live tapings, including apps, games and services that can be cheaply built with AI.
  • Tedesco: "This is not A.I. slop. This is not A.I. writing. This is a further progression of technology making creativity better and more accessible. This is a thing I wasn't able to build a year ago, and it's a thing that Sean wouldn't be able to, or maybe even want to, build himself." (Referring to a hypothetical bot serving The Ringer's Sean Fennessey's movie recommendations.)
  • Tedesco: "Let us build the tools to think about growth for you in what we think will be the highest-leverage way, not just the way that is generally recommended."
  • Tedesco on why creators default to known products: "You get into this hamster wheel and it's so hard to get off, because it takes a lot of resources, effort, time, and money."
  • Lenny Rachitsky created Product Pass last year, a Substack tier offering discounts on AI productivity tools. He valued the original bundle of roughly 25 tools at $25,000 in January; with new partnerships it is now valued at more than $30,000. The tier costs top subscribers $400 a year. Rachitsky has roughly 1.2 million total newsletter subscribers, with a smaller number on premium tiers. He has said the pass paid for itself for most subscribers after a couple of redemptions.
  • Emily Sundberg's Feed Me has introduced a job board for subscribers.
  • John Fulton's Los Angeles newsletter Eastside Rag hosted a subscriber singles-only event that drew more than 300 people, per The Atlantic.
  • Patreon found 81 percent of creators want a direct channel to their fans, and nearly 80 percent of fans said they would pay for access to a creator's community.
  • The New York Times is pursuing an AI-enabled internal archive search tool.
  • Every, an AI-focused newsletter and media company, has more than 130,000 readers on its "Chain of Thought" newsletter.

ABC Made Budget Cuts the Price of Renewing Jimmy Kimmel
Jimmy Kimmel Live! costs about what CBS paid to make Colbert's $100 million-a-year Late Show, and Disney's Debra OConnell opened the talks by telling Kimmel's agent to cut it.
Kimmel told ABC in late August he wants another season beyond the current deal, which ends in May, and he is working off one-year extensions rather than the usual three. Debra OConnell, who runs ABC, is negotiating with his agent James Dixon and has told him the budget must come down; a source close to the talks estimated 20 percent. Late night on ABC, CBS and NBC drew $221 million in ad revenue in 2024, half the $439 million of 2018. Kimmel's fee has been reported at $15 million. Disney is suing the FCC over its license review.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Kimmel is being asked to fund his own renewal out of the show's budget, and on one-year extensions that ask can return every spring.
The Facts
  • Jimmy Kimmel Live! produces at roughly the $100 million a year CBS was paying to make The Late Show With Stephen Colbert, per two sources cited by Puck.
  • CBS canceled Colbert's Late Show last fall, shortly before David Ellison's Skydance closed its $8 billion acquisition of Paramount. Belloni previously reported Late Show was losing about $40 million a year; Kimmel was among those who challenged that figure.
  • Kimmel's current deal ends in May. He began working off one-year extensions with this season rather than the more common three-year term.
  • Debra OConnell, chair of Disney Entertainment Television and lead executive over ABC, is negotiating with Kimmel's longtime agent James "Baby Doll" Dixon. Both sides say they want to make a deal.
  • The exact cut is undetermined. A strong source close to the situation told Puck that 20 percent of the current budget was a fair estimate. Disney and a rep for Kimmel declined to comment on that number.
  • Late-night ad revenue across ABC, CBS and NBC: $221 million in 2024, against $439 million in 2018. Puck reports the figure has declined further since and digital dollars have not made up the difference.
  • Kimmel's fee has been reported at $15 million a year. Belloni says he has not confirmed it.
  • Cost levers named: eliminating production weeks, going to full summer reruns in place of two months of guest-hosted shows, cutting writers, producers or staff, dropping costly stunts such as the Brooklyn taping week ABC approved for this fall, or reducing Kimmel's own fee.

YouTube Is Showing NFL Games Without Buying NFL Rights
YouTube ingested Peacock Premium into YouTube Premium in late July, delivering a full NFL season including postseason, plus NBA, MLB and the Olympics, without licensing a single game from the league.
Under a late-July agreement, YouTube pays Comcast an undisclosed wholesale fee per subscriber per month to carry Peacock Premium inside YouTube Premium, putting NFL games in front of tens of millions of YouTube subscribers with no rights deal and no production cost. LightShed notes the NFL has not said publicly whether its contracts permit this, since sublicensing NFL rights is contractually forbidden. The league holds options to exit or renegotiate with Paramount/CBS, Fox, NBC and Amazon after the 2029 season, and with ESPN after 2030. Existing partners have no right of first refusal.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A license is only worth what competing buyers must pay for it, and the anti-sublicensing clause is the term that decides whether a distributor has to bid at all or can reach the same audience through somebody else's deal.
The Facts
  • Roger Goodell, asked on CNBC Thursday whether the NFL would exercise its options to renegotiate media rights deals: "We don't have to make that decision today. That's the reason you have an option."
  • A year earlier Goodell had said renegotiation "could happen as early as next year [2026]."
  • Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch on last month's earnings call: "we will not be making any amendments to our existing [NFL] contractual relationship... We don't see any changes to our contractual terms until the 2030 season."
  • Three option sets: the Paramount/Skydance merger triggered a change of control letting the NFL exit or renegotiate with Paramount/CBS within two years of closing (by August 2027); Paramount/CBS, Fox, Comcast/NBC and Amazon agreements all carry an exit/renegotiate option after the 2029 season; Disney/ESPN after the 2030 season.
  • Goodell on repackaging: "One of the things we are doing as a league is talking to our partners, talking to future partners, potential partners, talking to others and evaluating, should we repackage our current packages?"
  • Netflix's multi-year package of 4 to 5 games per season runs through the 2029 season.
  • LightShed's risk case: if Netflix and Amazon replicate the YouTube/Peacock ingestion model, all three reduce their need to license NFL content directly and the bidder pool shrinks rather than grows.
  • LightShed expects the NFL to add language preventing bundling/ingestion when it triggers the 2029/2030 options.

Warner Bros Motion Picture chairs Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy sat with TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey on Friday and described their model as building repeat business with filmmakers. De Luca called credibility with filmmakers "the only currency that matters" and said the studio's job is to give a filmmaker an experience they can trust. Abdy said the industry is making 20 to 30 percent fewer movies than before the pandemic and declined to compare years, saying every movie is different. Domestic box office is tracking to $10 billion, which De Luca noted inflation dilutes.

The Facts
  • Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy, chairs of Warner Bros Motion Picture Group, spoke with TIFF CEO Cameron Bailey at the festival's new market on Friday, September 11. The pending Paramount Skydance acquisition was not raised by either side.

  • The studio won 11 Oscars this year from Sinners, Weapons and One Battle After Another, including Best Picture for the last, its first since Argo in 2012.
  • De Luca on credibility with filmmakers: "It's the only currency that matters." He compared a studio to a bank: "You can put a face on that and give the filmmaker an experience that they can trust, you get repeat business. People want to come back because they feel they were treated fairly."

  • De Luca said that when he and Abdy met WBD CEO David Zaslav about the job, they believed the theatrical audience was returning post-pandemic, contrary to the prior AT&T-era view that streaming was the future.
  • De Luca on Warner's legacy: "We talked about the legacy of Warner Bros. with socially relevant movies, and not trading commercial success for social relevance. Social relevance can be a commercial hook that gives your campaign a reason to be."
  • De Luca on the market: domestic box office is bound for its best post-Covid year at $10 billion, though inflation dilutes the real figure. "Our mission is to be a bigger piece of that smaller pie. The bar is high on quality control and curation."

Bartiromo Negotiated One Executive Out of Her Show and He Still Set the Guidance
Bartiromo renewed with Fox News Media in February 2025 with provisions that Fox Business programming chief Ralph Giordano would have no oversight of her show; in July he texted her producers to skip a Trump speech.
Puck reports that when Maria Bartiromo renewed with Fox News Media in February 2025, she asked for specific provisions ensuring Ralph Giordano, senior vice president of programming for Fox Business Network, would have no influence or oversight of her show, according to sources with knowledge of the negotiations. Giordano continued to exert influence through general editorial guidance, including a July 15 text telling her producers to forgo coverage of a Trump speech on election integrity. Fox and Bartiromo split last week, and she has hired Bryan Freedman to fight the terms of her dismissal.
Potential Talent Implication (New Revenue Stream): A provision that removes one named executive from a show does not reach the channels that executive still controls, so the term that decides creative autonomy is the one covering editorial guidance rather than reporting line or title.
The Facts
  • Bartiromo renewed with Fox News Media in February 2025 and asked for specific provisions ensuring Giordano would have no influence or oversight of her show, per sources with knowledge of the contract negotiations.
  • July 15: Giordano texted Bartiromo's producers, primarily executive producer Patrick Ignozzi, with guidance to forgo coverage of Trump's July 16 primetime speech on election integrity. Ignozzi forwarded it to Bartiromo.
  • Bartiromo had planned to cover the speech and to book Peter Navarro, a senior counselor to Trump.
  • Navarro told Byers that Bartiromo screenshotted the guidance and sent it to him, describing management as "censoring" the coverage, and that he passed it "up the chain" to senior administration officials.

Comedies Now Need a Plot Engine to Survive Their First Season

Florida Says Netflix Sold an Ad-Free Promise and Built an Ad Business
Florida's attorney general sued Netflix in state court Wednesday, alleging it collected roughly 550 billion events a day as early as 2016 and later monetized that data through the ad tier it launched in 2022.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier filed suit under state unfair and deceptive practices law, seeking damages and an order forcing Netflix to stop collecting and monetizing user data. The complaint says Netflix marketed itself as kid-friendly and ad-free, citing a 2019 shareholder letter calling the absence of ads "a deep part of our brand proposition," while logging some 550 billion events per day as early as 2016. It alleges autoplay was designed to extend viewing, and that advertisers can match their own data to Netflix profiles carrying education, marital status and household income. Netflix says it complies with privacy law.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Netflix's engagement data is the basis for every renewal and bonus decision a producer cannot audit, and a state action seeking to bar its collection puts a court, rather than a negotiation, on the question of what that data is and who it belongs to.
The Facts

Toronto's New Market Moves Indie Financing Three Months Earlier
The TIFF market runs September 10 to 16 with more than 150 exhibitors, and sellers told Deadline they will assemble finance plans this fall and start cameras in January.

Deadline reports AFM would become the place those contracts close.

The Facts
  • The TIFF market runs September 10 to 16 at the Metro Toronto Convention Centre with some 150-plus exhibitors.
  • Advisory committee members named by Deadline: CAA Media Finance co-head Roeg Sutherland, Mubi SVP global distribution Arianna Bocco, Sony Pictures Classics co-founder and co-president Michael Barker.
  • One indie label boss: "One of the frustrations out of [November's American Film Market] is that by the time you did presales to finance a project, those contracts aren't signed and I can't actually go to bank. I can't do anything until later next year. Whereas in Toronto, you can spend your fall putting your finance plan together and boom go into production at the start of January."

A Documentary That Names Its Abusers Is Harder to Sue
California's Second District Court of Appeal reversed the trial court on Thursday and dismissed Dan Schneider's defamation suit against Warner Bros. Discovery, Maxine Productions and Sony Pictures Television over Quiet on Set.
The panel found the docuseries "clearly distinguishes" between the gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior and sexual innuendo its participants attribute to Schneider and the child sexual abuse it attributes to three named individuals, and noted the series told viewers a Nickelodeon investigation found no evidence of abuse by him. A Los Angeles Superior Court judge had let the case proceed in 2024 after finding viewers could draw "damning implications." Schneider had sought damages and an order removing portions of the series or taking it down entirely. Gibson Dunn handled the appeal for Warner Bros.
Potential Talent Implication: A documentary that says plainly who did what is protected even where the editing invites a darker reading, which is what a filmmaker's insurer and its on-camera participants are relying on when they agree to name a living subject.
The Facts
  • California's Second District Court of Appeal ruled Thursday, September 10, reversing a 2024 decision by Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Ashfaq G. Chowdhury that had allowed the suit to proceed.
  • From the decision: "The documentary clearly distinguishes between the lamentable conduct that its participants attribute to Schneider, gender discrimination, harassment, toxic workplace behavior, and inappropriate sexual innuendo, and the child sexual abuse explicitly attributed to three named individuals."
  • The court said it would "refrain from splitting hairs to find an allegation of child sexual abuse where the only such abuse discussed is explicitly attributed to named perpetrators and the documentary expressly states that an investigation into Schneider found no evidence of abuse."
  • Schneider had targeted the editing: episode two introduces abusers Brian Peck and Jason Handy while cutting to images of Schneider. The panel reviewed the segment and found roughly six minutes focused on Handy with no time given to Schneider in those scenes.
  • "Schneider's attempt to find an alternative meaning than what is expressly stated in the documentary is unavailing," the order stated.
  • Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV debuted in 2024 on Max and Investigation Discovery. In episode three, Drake Bell came forward as the anonymous victim in the case against dialogue coach Brian Peck, convicted in 2004.
  • Defendants named in the complaint: Warner Bros. Discovery, Maxine Productions and Sony Pictures Television.
  • Warners' appeal was handled by Theodore J. Boutrous, Ilissa Samplin, Zachary C. Freund and Connor S. Sullivan of Gibson Dunn. The Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press and the International Documentary Association filed amicus briefs supporting the studio.
  • Schneider lawyer Gerry Silver said the producer is evaluating "options for further review and appeal."

Texas Has $1.5 Billion in Film Rebates and a Company Selling Help Claiming It
Goldenrod went live Thursday for Texas productions with pilots in Kentucky and Louisiana, charging a deposit plus a percentage of the incentive money it captures for film, television, commercial and game shoots.
The Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program passed last fall set a $1.5 billion fund paying $300 million every two years for a decade. The base rate runs 5% to 25% depending on in-state spend above a $250,000 minimum, with uplifts available, and it pays as a cash rebate, which lands faster than a tax credit. At least 60% of production must happen in state and 35% of cast and crew must be Texas residents. Co-founder Russell Wayne Groves said about 10 productions beta tested the service, whose founders include a former Texas Film Commission incentives lead.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A residency floor and an in-state spend floor decide whether a rebate pays at all, so the hiring plan and the shooting schedule are where a producer's incentive money is won or lost before a single term is negotiated.
The Facts
  • Goldenrod launched Thursday, September 10, live for Texas productions with pilot projects in Kentucky and Louisiana. It covers film, television, commercial and video game productions.
  • Business model: a deposit upfront plus a percentage of incentives captured.
  • The expanded Texas Moving Image Industry Incentive Program, passed last fall, established a $1.5 billion fund, or $300 million every two years for a decade.
  • Base incentive rate is 5% to 25% depending on in-state spend, with a $250,000 minimum and uplifts possible. It is a cash rebate system, which pays out faster than a tax incentive.
  • At least 60% of production must be completed in state. Texas has a 35% residency requirement for cast and crew.
  • Co-founder Russell Wayne Groves, founder of The Ranch Productions in Austin: "Incentives compliance is genuinely hard to get right. The administrative load pulls you off set, off the creative work, and if you miss something, you're either leaving significant dollars on the table or facing disqualification entirely." He compared the service to "a TurboTax for production incentives."
  • Groves on the residency math: "So, if you were at 30% and you were on week four of five, you'd... need to hire an extra five people to fit in that box. That is what we're trying to flag."
  • Other founders: Ted Griffis and Brandon Thomas of Austin post house TBD Post, and Tara Khanna, former Incentives Team Lead and Senior Production Incentives Specialist at the Texas Film Commission.
  • Groves onboarded his own SXSW-premiering film Stages first; about 10 productions beta tested.
  • Goldenrod has a list of about 16 more states to tap. "We're going to move extremely quickly after TIFF," Groves said.
  • Deadline notes Paramount CEO David Ellison named Texas last month as one of a few states he would consider for relocating the studio absent settlement talks in the antitrust suit led by California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

Ten States Have Pulled Back the Tax Breaks They Gave Data Centers
New Jersey cancelled $250 million in AI and data center credits in August, Illinois suspended its program for two years from July 1, and the governors of Ohio and Texas moved against their own exemptions.
Newsweek counted action across ten states. Illinois Governor JB Pritzker suspended new data center incentives for two years beginning July 1, 2026, to study energy demand, water use and electricity costs. Ohio Governor Mike DeWine paused new applications in May. Texas Governor Greg Abbott recommended repealing sales tax exemptions in June, arguing developers should cover more power and infrastructure costs. Virginia kept its exemption but added a tax of $0.011 per kilowatt hour on data center electricity. Minnesota repealed its electricity exemption effective July 2025. Arizona, Georgia and Michigan have bills pending; Washington narrowed its exemptions through Senate Bill 6231.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): State legislatures that spent a decade defending tech subsidies are now repealing them, which is the same political test a film and television incentive has to pass every session it comes up for renewal.
The Facts
  • Newsweek, published September 9, 2026, documents action in Arizona, Georgia, Illinois, Michigan, Minnesota, New Jersey, Ohio, Texas, Virginia and Washington.
  • New Jersey enacted the "End Data Center Tax Credits Act" in August 2026, eliminating the remaining $250 million available for AI and data center projects under the Next New Jersey Program.
  • Illinois: Governor JB Pritzker announced a two-year suspension of new data center incentives beginning July 1, 2026, to study energy demand, water use and electricity costs.
  • Ohio: Governor Mike DeWine paused new applications for the sales tax exemption in May 2026.
  • Texas: Governor Greg Abbott recommended repealing sales tax exemptions and other data center incentives in June 2026. No repeal has been enacted.
  • Virginia: Senator Danica Roem's proposed repeal (S.B. 30) projected roughly $1 billion in additional general fund revenue in year one and $1.1 billion in year two. It was not enacted; the 2026 budget compromise kept the exemption and added a $0.011 per kilowatt hour tax on data center electricity consumption.
  • Minnesota repealed the sales tax exemption for electricity used by qualified data centers, effective for purchases after June 30, 2025.
  • Washington's Senate Bill 6231 removed exemptions for replacement server equipment and ended eligibility for certain refurbished data centers, keeping incentives for qualifying new facilities.
  • Arizona Senate Bills 1463 and 1467 and House Bill 2820 would repeal the state's data center certification program. Georgia Senate Bill 410 would stop new exemption certificates. Michigan House Bills 5396 and 5398 target the sales tax exemption and property tax treatment. None has been enacted.
  • Newsweek reports the stated objections are electricity demand, water consumption, grid infrastructure costs and lost tax revenue, and that incentive programs have cost more than originally projected as AI demand grew. Newsweek says it contacted the Data Center Coalition for comment and was awaiting a response.

McClatchy Cut More Than 90 Journalists Months After Pushing Them Onto AI
Unions estimated more than 90 journalists lost jobs Thursday across at least 13 papers in eight states, including over 30 positions at the Miami Herald and a third of unionized staff in the Pacific Northwest.
An internal memo, first shared publicly by the New York Times' Katie Robertson, said consumer revenue fell 41% while local news expenses stayed flat, and that "the status quo no longer works." Earlier this year more than 30 Sacramento Bee staffers said they would withhold bylines from work produced by McClatchy's "content scaling agent," a generative tool that let editors republish reporters' existing work under new headlines. NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss said the 41% figure "needs to be verified." McClatchy did not respond to TheWrap and had made no public announcement as of Thursday afternoon.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): A tool that republishes a writer's existing work under new headlines is a use of that work, and the byline strike at the Sacramento Bee shows the credit is the only place a staff writer can price it.
The Facts
  • Layoffs hit McClatchy newsrooms nationwide on Thursday, September 10. Unions estimated more than 90 journalists affected across at least 13 papers in eight states.

  • The Pacific Northwest Newspaper Guild said it was "shocked and disappointed" by cuts to 33% of unionized workers at the Idaho Statesman, The News Tribune (Tacoma), Tri-City Herald, The Olympian and Bellingham Herald, including 10 journalists in Idaho and seven in Washington.
  • The Charlotte Observer reported eight employees laid off, about a quarter of its newsroom.
  • Internal memo, first shared publicly by New York Times reporter Katie Robertson: an internal analysis found consumer revenue declined 41% while local news expenses remained flat. "We are making these changes because the status quo no longer works. We cannot continue investing where subscriber interest does not support the investment."

  • Ariane Lange, investigative reporter and vice chair of the Bee's union, said management promoted the tool as a way to boost traffic and productivity, and that it allowed editors to produce repurposed versions of previous work under new headlines.
  • NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss said the 41% decline "needs to be verified," and wrote: "McClatchy execs decided to push AI slop on news sites. You can't pivot to AI, cut 40% of your local journalists and write 'we remain deeply committed to local journalism.' You're lying."
  • New York Times media reporter Ben Mullin: "This is one of the bleakest media layoff memos I've seen in 12 years covering the industry."
  • McClatchy is 168 years old and owns the Sacramento Bee, the Miami Herald and the Charlotte Observer among others. Representatives did not respond to TheWrap.

The Federal Film Credit Has Bill Language and No Time to Pass It
The working figure is a 20 percent credit that could rise another 5 to 10 points for rural filming or for spreading spend across states, and Congress leaves for the midterms within days.
Senator Adam Schiff's office told Deadline that bill language exists for a federal film and TV incentive and that Senate, House and Trump administration leaders are finalizing text. The working number is a 20 percent credit, rising at least 5 to 10 points for rural filming or spend spread across several states. Drafters modeled it on California's $750 million annual program, and some language comes from suggestions David Ellison put to members of Congress privately. Both chambers recess for the midterms in days, and the measure must clear the Joint Committee on Taxation.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Where the rate lands, 20 percent or 30 with the rural and multi-state bonuses, is the difference between a budget that can carry a star's quote domestically and one that goes overseas for the credit.
The Facts
  • Schiff spokesperson: "There is bill language, and currently, leaders in the Senate, House, and Trump administration are engaging in conversations to finalize text." And: "Negotiations are ongoing."
  • Working figure: 20 percent credit, plus at least 5 to 10 points for rural-area filming or spreading production spend across several states.
  • Bill name: the Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act, a Trump-coined title.
  • House sponsors: Linda Sanchez (D-CA, Ways and Means) and Laura Friedman (D-CA, ex-Rysher Entertainment, Schiff's successor in Burbank). Republicans Nathaniel Moran (R-TX) and Brian Jack (R-GA) are also in the mix.
  • Structure modeled on California's $750 million annual program, including a menu of redemption methods over several years. Relocation provision targets series or films first made outside the country, or content already assured foreign credits that has not started production.
  • Some draft language is lifted from suggestions made by Paramount CEO David Ellison in private meetings with members of Congress. Paramount did not respond to Deadline's request for comment.
  • Procedural gate: the measure must go to the Joint Committee on Taxation, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-ID), which reviews any tax credit initiative exceeding $2 million.
  • Timing: both chambers recess for the midterms within days; DC is expected to be empty from October to the second week of November. A GOP midterms mini-convention runs in Dallas from Wednesday.
  • Jon Voight's plan is the version Trump is backing.

Paramount Paid Over $100 Million for a Movie It Has Not Dated
Trey Parker and Matt Stone's untitled musical, known inside Paramount as Whitney Springs, was picked up in January 2022 as a negative pickup, lost two release dates and came off the schedule entirely last November.
Paramount committed more than $100 million to an untitled Trey Parker and Matt Stone feature through a negative pickup, a deal where the studio buys a finished film and the filmmakers keep whatever is left of the budget, Matthew Frank reported in The Ankler. One person familiar put the total at $150 million; another put it between $70 and $80 million. Kendrick Lamar and Dave Free produce and Lamar wrote original, unreleased songs. Paramount dated the picture for July 4, 2025, moved it to March 20, 2026, then took it off the schedule last November.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A negative pickup pays the filmmakers at delivery and lets them keep what they did not spend, so Parker and Stone have their nine-figure money while the picture sits undated and every part of a deal that pays on release stays unpaid.
The Facts
  • Project: untitled feature written by South Park veteran Vernon Chatman, directed by Trey Parker, produced by Matt Stone, Kendrick Lamar and Dave Free. Known internally at Paramount as Whitney Springs. Parker plays the town's mayor.
  • Premise: a musical comedy about reparations for slavery, set at a historical slave plantation museum in the Midwest, following a young Black re-enactor who clashes with the town's racist mayor.
  • Deal: "Paramount committed more than $100 million to the project through a negative pickup - where the creators keep what is left from the budget." One source put the total cost at $150 million; another put the deal terms between $70 and $80 million.
  • The budget was defrayed across multiple Paramount divisions, including Chris McCarthy's cable group. The film has no A-list cast or heavy visual effects; "whatever the filmmakers didn't spend, they kept."
  • Timeline: Paramount execs read the script at Park County in late 2021; the studio picked it up in January 2022. Then-Paramount Pictures head Brian Robbins called it "one of the funniest and most original scripts we've ever read" at CinemaCon 2024. Set for July 4, 2025; moved in March 2025 to March 20, 2026; removed from the schedule in November 2025; unmentioned at David Ellison's first CinemaCon in April 2026.
  • Statement from Stone and Parker: "We take full responsibility for the schedule delay of this movie. We apologize to our partners at pgLang and Paramount and we appreciate their patience. South Park and life's circumstances have gotten in the way but we still believe in the project."
  • Paramount declined to comment; pgLang did not respond.
  • People close to the production called Lamar's music among the strongest elements and described early cuts as "really rough." No source said Ellison ordered a delay over the film's politics.
  • Context: Parker and Stone's five-year, $500-$550 million HBO Max streaming deal expired in 2025; after a public fight they signed a five-year, $1.5 billion contract for South Park streaming rights plus 10 new episodes a year in July 2025.
  • Comparable undated comedies: Warner Bros.' Animal Friends with Ryan Reynolds, pushed four times, most recently to January 22, 2027; Jonah Hill's Cut Off, pulled from July 17 with no new date.
  • Paramount has 12 films dated for 2027 and seven for 2028.

Creators Wrote Their Own AI Definitions Before the Studios Did
The Standards & Definitions Project launched Wednesday with a glossary of about 180 AI terms and a visualizer scoring roughly 150 creative jobs from 0 to 5 on AI replacement.
The Creators Coalition on AI, founded nine months ago by Joseph Gordon-Levitt, Daniel Kwan and late-night veteran Ted Tremper, launched a public Standards & Definitions Project on Wednesday. It carries a glossary of roughly 180 AI terms and an AI Impact Visualizer rating about 150 jobs across 11 creative areas, including directing, sound, animation, writing and acting, from 0 (does not touch the job) to 5 (could do the whole job). More than 250 people have been polled and most roles still read "required knowledge." Founders say the shared terms are meant for guild negotiations and individual talent deals.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Human-authored content and AI digital performance now have written definitions that did not come off a studio's paper, and those are the terms a deal about AI use will be argued in.
The Facts
  • Launch date: Wednesday, September 9, 2026. Project name: the Standards & Definitions Project, run by the Creators Coalition on AI (CCAI).
  • Glossary: approximately 180 AI terms.
  • AI Impact Visualizer: about 150 jobs across 11 creative areas, scored 0 to 5 on likelihood of AI role replacement. Many roles broken into dozens of sub-categories.
  • More than 250 people polled to date; the project targets responses in the thousands. Major updates planned quarterly. A survey page vets users to confirm they work in Hollywood.
  • CCAI founded December 2025 by Gordon-Levitt, Kwan, Ted Tremper and more than a dozen others. Thousands of signatories including Judd Apatow, Ava DuVernay, Margot Robbie, Guillermo del Toro and Hiro Murai. David Goyer is a founder and the group's secretary.
  • Two conventions were held this summer with guild-based delegates from all 11 areas; the most recent concluded ten days before launch.
  • Sample definition, human-authored content: "Creative work in which no generative AI system contributed expressive content, irrespective of the technological tools otherwise used in its creation, capture, processing, or distribution."
  • Sample definition, AI Digital Performance: "the application of artificial intelligence to capture, synthesize, modify, and/or replicate a human being or animal performer's natural person's human individual's performance attributes, which can include visual and physiological likeness, both still and kinetic facial expression, body movement, biometric characteristics, choreography, and voice whether partially or in full."
  • Tremper: "The purpose of these resources is take all the things we hear about with regard to AI and establish ground truth." He also cited a use case in drafting statehouse bills.
  • Gordon-Levitt: "Artists and content creators are a canary in the coal mine."
  • Kwan: "If we're going to be fighting for transparency, we should also be modeling it."

Imax Is Putting Up the Capital to Take a Bigger Share of the Box Office
Imax has passed $600 million in global box office this quarter against a previous best in the mid-$300 millions, and Rich Gelfond said The Odyssey is nearing $500 million in Imax receipts on about 1% of the world's screens.
Rich Gelfond told the Goldman Sachs Communacopia conference that Imax screens have passed $600 million in global box office receipts this quarter, against a best-ever quarter in the mid-$300 millions in 2023. Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey is approaching $500 million in Imax receipts, more than double the $230 million Avatar drew on its initial run, on roughly 1% of the world's screens. Imax keeps about 18 cents of every box office dollar and has moved from licensing its technology toward a joint venture model where it supplies more of the capital for a larger share of the gross.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Gelfond said Imax's primary relationships are with filmmakers and that wherever they end up is who Imax talks to about content, which makes an Imax commitment a piece of leverage a director holds independent of whichever studio owns the picture after a merger.
The Facts

  • Gelfond: "When we looked at our slate for the year, I was the most bullish person in the company on The Odyssey."
  • Economics: "Imax splits the box office take with movie theaters and sometimes studios depending the structure of the exhibitor deal, getting about 18 cents on the dollar."
  • Model shift, in Gelfond's words: "Our old model used to be, [exhibitors] would put up all the money and we would license our technology. Then we went more to a joint venture model, where we take a bigger percentage of the box office, but we put up more of the capital ... Jordan, in March. Sony's four Beatles films start rolling out in 2028, with Joseph Kosinski's Miami Vice '85.

Channel 4 will cut roughly 340 roles, 28 percent of its workforce, by the end of 2026. Netflix will publish grosses for La Bola Negra, Mosquito Bowl, David Fincher's The Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth, Danny Boyle's Ink, Greta Gerwig's Narnia: The Magician's Nephew and Charlie and the Chocolate Factory. The windows run 46, 26, 27, 27, 50 and 47 days. The Draft Federal Film Credit Covers Star Pay, Not Just Crew
The base credit is 20 percent of all labor costs above and below the line, four optional uplifts of five percent each take it to 30, and it stacks on state incentives to 60 percent or more.
Reps. Nathaniel Moran and Linda Sanchez, both on House Ways and Means, are drafting a federal film and television incentive expected to be introduced this month. The base credit covers 20 percent of all labor costs, above the line as well as below. Producers can claim up to two of four five percent uplifts: rural opportunity zones, independent productions, repatriated filming, or $10 million spent across ten states. Reality TV and animation qualify, news and sports do not. Producers can sell the credit but cannot claim a refund.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): A federal credit that covers above-the-line labor makes star, director and writer compensation a subsidized line in the budget rather than the line a studio cuts first to make a picture work in a cheaper territory.
The Facts
  • Base credit: 20 percent of all labor costs, both below-the-line and above-the-line.
  • Four uplifts of five percent each: filming in a rural opportunity zone; an independent production; bringing a certain amount of filming back to the U.S. from abroad; spending at least $10 million in ten different states in a year. Producers may claim up to two, for a maximum of 30 percent.
  • The federal credit stacks on state incentives, which supporters say could total 60 percent or more depending on location.
  • Eligible: films, scripted TV, reality TV and animation. Not eligible: news and sports broadcasts.
  • The credit can offset federal income tax or be sold to another taxpayer. It is not refundable.
  • Drafters: Rep. Nathaniel Moran (R-Texas) and Rep. Linda Sanchez (D-Calif.), both on House Ways and Means. Rep. Laura Friedman (D-Calif.) and Rep. Brian Jack (R-Ga.) also working on it.
  • The bill is expected to be introduced this month, possibly by the end of next week.
  • Trump endorsed a federal incentive in a Truth Social post on August 31.
  • The draft broadly aligns with the Motion Picture Association's request. The MPA and entertainment unions have been advocating for a year.
  • A California proposal for a bonus in federally declared disaster zones, which would cover all of Los Angeles County after the 2025 fires, is not in the current draft.
  • The bill has not gone to the Joint Committee on Taxation for a cost score. Variety reports the cost will run into the billions.
  • Friedman: "I would be very happy for it to happen in the lame duck. I can't promise that's possible."
  • Friedman on Trump's involvement: "I can't tell you the number of texts that have come in from people who have offered to help."

Family Offices Put $22.2 Billion Into Media in Two Years
FINTRX counted 137 investments across 123 media and entertainment companies since 2024, from Access Industries' $827 million in DAZN to TWG Global's $10 billion for the Los Angeles Lakers.
TheWrap reported that family offices, the private firms managing assets for one family or a small group, have become a direct financing route into entertainment. FINTRX, a private wealth data platform, counted 137 investments across 123 media and entertainment portfolio companies over two years, worth $22.2 billion, plus 22 follow-on investments. Wealth advisor Kerry Finn of Sequoia Sentinel said checks often run $1 million to $5 million across multiple projects rather than one large commitment. Julie Zorn, head of CAA's Global Family Office Advisory, said families are building verticals in sports, entertainment and media.
Potential Talent Implication (Company Building): Kerry Finn's clients are writing $1 million to $5 million checks across multiple projects and Julie Zorn says the families are building their own entertainment verticals, so the capital behind a talent-owned company now sits outside both the studios and the banks.
The Facts
  • FINTRX count over two years: 137 investments, 123 media and entertainment portfolio companies, $22.2 billion aggregate value, plus 22 follow-on investments.
  • Split by year: 37 in 2024, 65 in 2025, 35 between January and July 1, 2026.
  • Largest disclosed: $827 million into DAZN from Len Blavatnik's Access Industries; $10 billion into the Los Angeles Lakers from TWG Global, the family office of Mark Walters.
  • Single family office economics: launched at roughly $100 million net worth, $500,000 to $5 million a year to operate; Kerry Finn puts the range at $100 million to $250 million investable and $250 million to $500 million net worth.
  • Multi-family office: roughly $25 million to $250 million investable. Virtual family office: roughly $5 million to $40 million investable.
  • Lou Taylor, Tri Star Sports and Entertainment Group: "If you're an actor in Hollywood making $3 million a year, it's not cost effective for you to set up your own family office."
  • Entertainment services cited: structuring income streams, residuals and royalties, back-end participation planning, loan-out corporation management, production company acquisition or exit planning, slate financing and co-investments.
  • Carolyn Hunt, Barnes & Thornburg: family offices "are not managing outside limited-partner capital and generally face far less quarterly reporting pressure than private equity firms, hedge funds or banks."
  • Finn on allocation: on $100 million liquid, 20 to 30 percent may go to alternatives, so up to $30 million across IP, film deals and similar.
  • FINTRX database: roughly 4,500 family offices, more than 30,000 contacts, $50 million minimum asset threshold.

British Producers Now Take More Money From Abroad Than From UK Broadcasters
UK broadcaster revenue fell 4.7 percent to £1.99 billion while international revenue rose 15.8 percent to £1.57 billion, and subscription streamers now place 72.3 percent of primary commissions from outside the UK.
The Pact Census for 2025 puts total UK independent producer revenue at £3.81 billion, up 4.1 percent, its second-highest total. UK television revenue fell 4.7 percent to £1.99 billion, below £2 billion for the first time since 2020 and a third consecutive year of decline. International revenue rose 15.8 percent to £1.57 billion, 41.1 percent of the total. The secondary rights market grew £65 million to £575 million. Pact chief executive Warner said broadcasters now contribute considerably less of the initial production cost, making retained rights more important to producers financing their own shows.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): UK producers now fund more of the budget themselves and recoup through the secondary rights market, and the Terms of Trade that let them keep those rights on a British commission are what Channel 4, Sky, ITV and the BBC are all reopening.
The Facts
  • Total UK independent producer revenue 2025: £3.81 billion, up 4.1 percent, second-highest on record behind 2022's just under £4 billion.
  • UK television revenue: £1.99 billion, down 4.7 percent from £2.09 billion, below £2 billion for the first time since 2020.
  • International revenue: £1.57 billion, up 15.8 percent from £1.35 billion, 41.1 percent of total revenue, second only to 2022's £1.62 billion.
  • Subscription streamers now account for 72.3 percent of all primary commissions from outside the UK, £916 million, up from 27 percent a decade ago.
  • Secondary rights market: up £65 million to £575 million.
  • Non-TV revenue (online publishing, talent management, promotions, PR, feature films): £258 million, above the previous record of £236 million set in 2013.
  • Domestic network commissions have fallen for a third consecutive year, pressuring small and mid-sized production companies.
  • Causes cited: advertising market contraction, viewer shift away from broadcast, inflationary production costs.
  • The Terms of Trade, in place since 2003, let independent producers retain rights to shows commissioned by British networks. Channel 4 is working on an in-house division, Sky is buying ITV, and BBC Director General Matt Brittin has questioned whether the rules remain fit for purpose.
  • Pact closed a new Terms of Trade deal with Paramount's Channel 5 in March.
  • Pact CEO Warner on secondary rights growth: "It could also suggest that producers might be increasingly relying on future rights revenue to help finance production."
  • Warner on financing: "In an environment where indies are contributing ever more towards the cost of production in the first place, they need to be in the position to recoup that investment themselves, and the rights become even more important."
  • The BBC is seeking up to £500 million in cost savings. Pact again proposed replacing the licence fee with a household levy on the German model.
  • Warner replaced long-serving CEO John McVay in March 2026.

Christine Is Stuck Inside Three Bankruptcies and Nobody Can Say Who Owns It
Rebecca Hall's 2016 drama is not being licensed to streamers or cable until a chain of title is re-established, and its filmmakers say they cannot get an answer from trustees in two countries.
Christine, the 2016 drama starring Rebecca Hall as news anchor Christine Chubbuck, is caught in overlapping bankruptcies and cannot be licensed. Distributor The Orchard became 1091 Media in 2019 when Sony divested, was bought by Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment in 2022, and went into Chapter 7 liquidation two years later. The filmmakers then learned the film's London financier Great Point Media had also gone bankrupt after founder Jim Reeve's death. Writer-producer Craig Shilowich says some or all of the rights sit inside the case and that trustees in two countries will not respond.
Potential Talent Implication (Rights Ownership): Christine built an audience on Netflix and is now unlicensable because no one can establish who holds the rights, which is what a reversion trigger tied to a distributor's insolvency exists to prevent.
The Facts
  • Christine premiered at Sundance in 2016. The Orchard bought U.S. distribution rights. It was nominated for Independent Spirit honors and won critics group prizes.
  • Hall: "It feels terrible because this is definitely a film and a performance that I'm incredibly proud of, and I know that it means a lot to a lot of people. So the idea that it could just sort of disappear is insane to me."
  • Hall on the release: "They didn't have the resources to capitalize on the acclaim and the other accolades that the film received. They just couldn't afford to market it in a big way, so the release suffered from that."
  • The Orchard ran a filmmaker portal showing box office plus digital sales and rentals. Shilowich: "They were like 'this is our thing, we're going to demystify film accounting.' They had a portal for filmmakers where you could see all the receipts coming in and out, and that was rare."
  • 2019: The Orchard rebranded as 1091 Media; principal backer Sony divested. The portal began going down frequently. Shilowich: "It became a promise that they didn't keep over time."
  • 2022: Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment bought 1091 Media and its library.
  • 2024: Chicken Soup for the Soul Entertainment failed and entered Chapter 7 liquidation.
  • The filmmakers then discovered Great Point Media, the London-based financier of Christine, had gone bankrupt following founder Jim Reeve's death.
  • Shilowich: "There was essentially no one to talk to about the fate of our film except for government-appointed bankruptcy trustees in two different countries. And there are a bunch of other smaller distribution outlets, like Redbox, the DVD kiosk company, involved. So it's actually a very large, extremely complex bankruptcy case, and some or all of our rights are involved."
  • Shilowich on trying to buy it back: "If the creditors aren't claiming it, I want to know, 'Well, can I have it? Can I buy it?' We're not only unable to get a satisfactory answer, but really to receive any response."
  • Until a chain of title is re-established, Christine, which previously built an audience on Netflix, is not being licensed to streamers or cable.
  • Director Antonio Campos: "I had this naive belief that when you sold your film to some place, they would take care of it. The person that's going to care the most about your work is you."
  • The filmmakers have spoken with other filmmakers whose work is caught in the same bankruptcies.
  • A tenth anniversary screening was held at Telluride, with additional screenings at Brooklyn's Nitehawk Cinema and the Jacob Burns Film Center.

Streaming Is Raising Prices Faster Than Cable Ever Did
Apple TV's price has tripled since 2019, Disney+ is up 172 percent, and eight ad free major streamers now cost about $151 a month against $90 four years ago.
The Hollywood Reporter compared streamer pricing against Bureau of Labor Statistics data and found streaming rates rose 11.8 percent over the past twelve months, against an annual average of 3.9 percent for cable and satellite. Since 2022, streaming prices have risen more than three times as fast as inflation. Apple TV launched at $4.99 in 2019 and now costs $15, half of that increase coming in the past year. Peacock's tiers rose about 50 percent. HBO Max is the outlier, up 23 percent over six years.

  • Apple TV: launched at $4.99 in 2019, now $15. Up 200 percent, with a 50 percent rise in the past year alone.
  • Disney+: launched at $6.99 with no ads in 2019, now $11.99 with ads. Up 172 percent on launch price.
  • Paramount+: cheapest tier up 80 percent in five years.
  • Netflix Premium: up 125 percent since 2013.
  • Peacock: tiers up roughly 50 percent recently. HBO Premium is $3 more than Peacock Premium Plus.
  • HBO Max: up 23 percent over six years, the smallest increase in the set.
  • Eight major streamers without ads or bundle commitments: about $151 a month, versus roughly $90 four years ago.
  • Consumer prices have risen an average of 3.84 percent annually since 2019, a 33 percent cumulative increase in cost of living.
  • Fully loaded cable bundles from Spectrum and DirecTV run north of $170 a month.

The Summer Box Office Hit $4.76 Billion and Admissions Rose With It
US summer box office reached an all-time record $4.76 billion, with admissions above 322 million against 275 million last summer, the first summer where all four core months each cleared $1 billion.
Rentrak has the May 1 to September 7 domestic frame at $4.76 billion, the highest on record, with each core month topping $1 billion for the first time. Price alone does not explain it: EntTelligence counts admissions above 322 million against 275 million in summer 2025, on an average adult ticket of $13.46. Universal led distributors at $1.23 billion, up 63 percent, ahead of Disney at $1.034 billion and Sony at $1 billion. Greenlight Analytics says the top 15 fall titles track 3.5 points ahead of last year.
Potential Talent Implication (Project Economics): Theatrical grosses grew on attendance rather than ticket-price inflation, so box office bonuses, cash breakeven and first-dollar-gross definitions are being negotiated against a market that is genuinely larger, and the two biggest breakouts were directed by filmmakers who came from YouTube.
The Facts
  • Record domestic summer of $4.76 billion for May 1 to September 7, per Rentrak. Variety separately reported the figure as $4.67 billion.
  • First summer on record where each of the four core months cleared $1 billion: May $1.07B, June $1.08B, July $1.18B, August $1.276B.
  • Admissions above 322 million versus summer 2025's 275 million, per EntTelligence. Average ticket prices: adult $13.46, child $11.51, adult premium large format $18.39.
  • Distributor share for the period: Universal $1.23B (+63%), Disney $1.034B (-2%), Sony $1B (+459%), Lionsgate $270M (+296%), Warner Bros $239.3M (-76%), Paramount $219.8M (-21%), Amazon MGM $170.1M (+400%).
  • Top 10 domestic: Spider-Man: Brand New Day (Sony) $923.2M; The Odyssey (Universal) $589M; Toy Story 5 (Disney) $479.9M; Obsession (Focus) $263.4M; Michael (Lionsgate) $242.5M summer, $372.3M lifetime; The Devil Wears Prada 2 (Disney) $220.6M; Backrooms (A24) $197.5M; Minions & Monsters (Universal) $183.1M; Star Wars: Mandalorian & Grogu (Disney) $177.7M; Moana (Disney) $126.2M.
  • Backrooms gave A24 both its biggest opening ever at $81.4 million and its highest-grossing title ever at $197.5 million. Michael became Lionsgate's highest-grossing film ever and passed $1 billion worldwide.
