The Paramount settlement everyone wants collides with the deal's own financing math
Warner Bros. and Paramount already have 35 films dated for 2027 as separate competitors, five above the 30-film floor being offered as merger protection.
CEO Summary
Joseph M. Singer, a former investment banker and slate film financier who discloses he has written against the merger, argues in The Hollywood Reporter that the settlement terms under discussion cannot coexist with the transaction's financing. The parties describe an enterprise value of $111 billion, leaving the combined company more than $80 billion in debt, roughly $3 billion in annual free cash flow, and a synergy target above $6 billion. Synergy means combining functions; a settlement requiring separate operations forgoes it.
Why This Matters
Singer checks the most concrete commitment against Rentrak's release calendars. Warner Bros. has 19 films scheduled for 2027 and Paramount has 16. The 30-film pledge Paramount has offered AMC, Regal and other chains sits below that combined figure, and the offered term runs three years, expiring roughly when integration completes.

The pledge is being scored against zero rather than against what the two studios already planned to release.
Specific Implication
Singer names the mechanisms that would make guarantees hold: escrowed funds, funded rather than pledged guarantees, more equity and less debt. Any party seeking output or employment protections should ask which of those is on the table.
The Facts
  • Deal economics as described by the parties: enterprise value $111 billion; more than $80 billion of debt on the combined company; roughly $3 billion in annual free cash flow; investment-grade commitment within a few years; synergy target above $6 billion.
  • The concrete commitment on the table: at least 30 theatrical releases a year, offered in writing to AMC, Regal and now other chains, potentially backed by penalties. The offered term runs three years.
  • Per Rentrak's release calendars: Warner Bros. has 19 films scheduled for 2027, Paramount has 16. For 2028 the two already have 22 films dated with slates still filling in.
  • Who wants a settlement: twelve state attorneys general, the Directors Guild and IATSE jointly, Cinema United, the three largest exhibitors, Gov. Gavin Newsom, likely successor Xavier Becerra and L.A. Mayor Karen Bass.
  • The Writers Guild's objection differs in kind: combining two major employers of writers reduces competition for writing services.
  • On synergies, Singer distinguishes benign savings (one software license, one headquarters lease) from those that eliminate a job, project, contract or line of spending, and asks which kind adds up to more than $6 billion at two companies that have already spent years cutting.
  • Los Angeles County's analysis identified thousands of exposed positions. Singer says his own analysis puts exposure considerably higher. Paramount argues a combined company would protect jobs better than two weaker ones.
  • Enforcement mechanisms Singer names: escrowed funds, funded rather than pledged guarantees, more equity and less debt. He observes each is available, each changes the deal's economics, and none has been offered.
  • One alternative he raises: Paramount owning both companies without integrating them.
  • Competitive spend benchmark cited: Netflix spends $20 billion a year on content.

CEO Summary
Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird said Tuesday she plans to take California directly to the U.S. Supreme Court over its antitrust challenge to Paramount's acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery. Writing in the Daily Wire, Bird argued that twelve states have overridden the judgment of the rest of the country and that Congress bars Iowa from suing California in district court. If oral argument were scheduled between October 2026 and April 2027, a decision would not come until late June or early July.
Why This Matters
Bird's own argument sets the price. She writes that Paramount owes Warner Bros. Discovery roughly $7 million a day from October while the deal sits in limbo, and that the trial the twelve attorneys general have engineered does not begin until March 2027. The Supreme Court route she describes would resolve months after that. The remedy she proposes runs longer than the delay she is objecting to.
The Facts
  • Bird announced Tuesday she plans to bring California directly to the U.S. Supreme Court, publishing the plan as an op-ed in the Daily Wire.
  • Jurisdictional argument: "California is once again trying to be the country's regulator... That makes this a dispute between states, and the Constitution says those can only be heard in the U.S. Supreme Court." She adds that "Iowa cannot sue California in a district court, because Congress said so."
  • On the twelve-state coalition: "twelve states have overridden that judgment for the entire country, and Iowans never got a vote."

Australia barred wholly AI-generated tracks from its charts and will make labels declare AI use
The rule takes effect Friday and follows an AI cover of Madonna's "Like a Prayer" that reached No. 4 on an ARIA singles chart.
CEO Summary
The Australian Recording Industry Association updated its charts code of practice to bar wholly AI-generated songs from its weekly charts and from ARIA Music Awards eligibility. Music made with generative AI qualifies only if it is "substantially human made" and "raises no stream or chart manipulation concerns." Tracks that used AI as a tool remain eligible. ARIA will require labels to mark each release as AI-generated or AI-assisted, using the taxonomy proposed last month by the IFPI and the RIAA.
Why This Matters
Enforcement sits with the distributor. ARIA has acknowledged it can identify generative-AI use only when a label tells it, so the rule works as a warranty the supplier signs rather than a test the chart runs.

Liability moves with the file. A label that certifies a release incorrectly loses chart and awards eligibility at once.
Specific Implication
Anyone drafting an AI clause should note who certifies here: the obligation, and the penalty, land on the delivering party rather than on the platform.
The Facts
  • The change takes effect Friday, via an update to the ARIA Charts code of practice.
  • Wholly AI-generated songs are barred from ARIA's weekly charts and from ARIA Music Awards eligibility.
  • Generative-AI music charts only if "substantially human made" and if it "raises no stream or chart manipulation concerns."
  • Songs where AI was used as a tool stay eligible.
  • ARIA will mandate the AI-generated and AI-assisted labels proposed last month by industry bodies including the IFPI and the RIAA.
  • Trigger: an AI cover of Madonna's "Like a Prayer" charted for weeks, reaching No. 4 on the Top 20 Australian Singles chart.
  • ARIA CEO Annaelle Herd: "Artists already use AI tools in their work, the Charts can and should evolve to keep room for that, but music generated wholesale by services built on artists' recordings is a different matter."
  • Herd: "a chart that rewards unlicensed AI output would undercut the very basis of the recorded music we exist to represent."
  • Per The Verge, ARIA admits it can only detect AI usage if "you tell us."
  • The move follows IFPI guidance last month for charts it manages across Latin America, the Middle East, Africa and Southeast Asia, requiring music to be mostly human-made, free of manipulation concerns, and made on an AI service that is "properly authorised and lawful."
  • In the U.S., AI-generated music has appeared on Billboard's Hot Gospel Songs and Hot R&B charts.
  • Universal Music Group, Warner Music Group and Sony Music demanded a comparable framework last month, seeking "a clear boundary between human-led creativity and works that are purely synthetic or generated by unauthorized AI models."

The company is moving up toward independent features budgeted at $10 million to $20 million. O'Hara described the aim as optimizing the business rather than one production at a time, and the structure follows: development, production, post and international partnerships inside one company. At this budget level financiers underwrite completion risk, meaning whether the film gets finished on budget, more than creative risk, and an integrated pipeline is how a company argues its budgets will hold.
Specific Implication
Talent considering these projects is looking at Southeast Asian shoots, which changes location terms, crew composition and travel provisions in the deal.

  • Macur: "We recognize that the independent film business is changing rapidly. Our response isn't to wait for the market to become predictable."

Discovery merger would not achieve its stated goal of preserving competitive health in theatrical film and basic cable. Why This Matters
Shapiro notes the redacted complaint does not mention AI once. Any structural remedy the states win would bind the combined company across a production-cost base and a discovery layer that generative tools are widely expected to reshape inside the remedy's own life.

He also reports that the Justice Department closed an eight-month review of more than two million documents without finding likely harm to competition in theatrical film, linear television or streaming, and that AMC, Regal and Cinemark all support the deal. That leaves the states defending a market structure its own buyers decline to defend.
Specific Implication
Anyone modeling release-date competition should weigh Shapiro's point that studios already clear space around rivals' tentpoles, which means consolidation may change actual scheduling behavior less than the concentration math implies.

'Obsession' Crossed $500 Million Worldwide on a Sub-$1 Million Budget, the First Original Film of the 2020s to Get There
Focus Features acquired Curry Barker's "Obsession" out of a festival for a reported $15 million, and it has now grossed $501.5 million worldwide.
CEO Summary
Focus Features' horror film "Obsession" has finished its domestic run at $263.4 million and reached $501.5 million worldwide. It passes Pixar's "Elemental" at $494.6 million to become the top grossing original film since the pandemic. Writer-director Curry Barker made it for under $1 million. It opened to $17.1 million domestically and did not fall below that weekend figure until its sixth weekend in release. South Korea has not opened yet.
Why This Matters
Focus paid about $15 million for finished rights, The Ankler reported, roughly fifteen times the production cost. Sellers heading into Toronto and the fall markets have that number now.

What the money did not buy is the hold. Weekend grosses that climbed above the opening for a month came from audience word of mouth, and that is the variable no buyer can read off a festival screening.
Specific Implication
Sellers with a finished genre title should expect buyers to answer the "Obsession" comp by tying more of the price to performance, through escalators and box office bonuses rather than a larger guarantee.

  • TheWrap: highest grossing festival acquisition of all time, and the highest grossing film ever made for under $1 million.
  • The Ankler: Focus acquired it for $15 million; $37 million of the worldwide gross comes from territories Universal does not hold; second biggest R-rated horror film ever, behind "IT."
  • Domestic opening $17.1 million. Weekend totals ran higher than the opening for the following month and stayed above $17 million through five weekends.
  • Released May 15 by Focus Features. Luminate's 2026 domestic chart ranks it 7th for the year at $263,451,720.
  • Barker's next film, "Anything but Ghosts," is set at Focus with Bryce Dallas Howard, Aaron Paul and Violet McGraw.

Three Former Child Stars Asked Where the Union Is After the Deaths of Hayden Panettiere, Michelle Trachtenberg and Daveigh Chase
Melissa Gilbert asked where the union, the regulations and the protection of privacy are, after three former child performers died before turning 40.
CEO Summary
Anna Paquin, Christy Carlson Romano and Melissa Gilbert each published statements this week calling for changes to how the industry treats child performers. Hayden Panettiere died last Sunday at 36, Michelle Trachtenberg died in February 2025 at 39, and Daveigh Chase died in July at 35. All three writers began working as children. Paquin wrote that the systems meant to protect them "look great on paper."
Why This Matters
Three separate statements in one week is the shape a labor issue takes before it becomes a bargaining item. Gilbert named the union directly, which moves the argument from public sympathy toward a contract that reopens on a schedule. Paquin's description of productions that handled young performers well points at the same place, because a practice one production adopts voluntarily is a practice that can be written down.
Specific Implication
Productions casting minors should expect on-set welfare and privacy terms to be raised in negotiation ahead of the next contract cycle rather than treated as a settled legal minimum.
The Facts
  • Paquin, on Instagram Friday: "It's not a coincidence that so many former, specifically pre-sexualized female, child 'stars' have profoundly sad lives and untimely ends. We were not as protected by the 'systems' that look great on paper, as we are supposed to be."
  • Paquin, in a second post, said she has worked on productions where the welfare and mental health of young performers was handled carefully, including around intense material: "It just has to be the top priority of the production."
  • Gilbert, on Substack Saturday: "Where is our Union in all of this? Where is the collective outrage? Where are the regulations? Where is the protection of privacy?"
  • Gilbert also wrote that the industry "uses, abuses, exploits and then throws away it's youngest, but for some reason, this trend is getting worse."
  • Romano, in an Elle essay earlier in the week, compared early fame to repeated-impact brain injury: "We now have language for youth sports: protocols, helmets, parents worried about concussions. But we have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood."

Taylor Sheridan and Paramount Are Sued Over Yellowstone's Origins by a Writer Who Pitched His Management Company in 2016
Salkin's suit says Elevate told her Sheridan was unavailable for TV projects, that Yellowstone was greenlit within months, and that two actors named in her pitch deck were later cast.
CEO Summary
Writer Lauren J. Salkin sued Taylor Sheridan on Friday over the origins of Yellowstone. Her complaint alleges she pitched a Western drama called Sovereign Nation to Sheridan's management company, Elevate Entertainment, in 2016, and was told he was unavailable for television. Paramount, 101 Studios and Elevate are also named as defendants. Representatives for Sheridan, Paramount, 101 Studios and Elevate did not immediately respond to Variety's request for comment.
Why This Matters
The complaint does not rest on Western tropes. It lists specific expressive choices, among them a tribal casino as the seat of political and development power, and trust land plus a 99-year lease structure as the mechanism of expansion, then argues those combine with access and timing to support an inference of copying.

One allegation resists a genre defense. Salkin says her pitch deck proposed Danny Huston and Gil Birmingham, and both were later cast in what the suit calls materially parallel structural roles.
Specific Implication
A pitch delivered to a producer's management company creates a dated record of access, and access is the element these claims are built on. Submission logs and rejection correspondence are the evidence on both sides of that question.
The Facts
  • Plaintiff: writer Lauren J. Salkin. Suit filed Friday, August 21, 2026.
  • Defendants: Taylor Sheridan, Paramount, 101 Studios, Elevate Entertainment.
  • Alleged 2016 pitch: a Western drama titled Sovereign Nation, submitted to Elevate Entertainment, Sheridan's management company.
  • Alleged rejection language, per the complaint: "Taylor thanks you very much for your interest. Unfortunately, he's unavailable for TV projects."
  • The suit states Yellowstone was greenlit at Paramount "within months" of that rejection. Paramount Network aired the first episode on June 20, 2018.
  • Alleged overlapping expressive choices: a tribal casino as the institutional center of political and development power; a confrontation staged in the tribal chairman's casino office over expansion beyond reservation boundaries; trust land, absence of zoning restrictions and a 99-year lease as the expansion mechanism; recurring master-plan imagery.
  • Casting allegation: Salkin's pitch deck proposed Danny Huston and Gil Birmingham; both were later cast in Yellowstone, Birmingham as the tribal political leader and Huston as an outside development power broker.
  • Complaint's stated standard: "These are not merely convergences of a shared genre. Taken together with access and timing, they support a strong inference of copying."

Cinema United, the DGA, IATSE and now Bass all represent people who earn money when productions run, and a year of corporate limbo costs them whether the case is won or lost. Any organization whose members are paid per production is a candidate to shift toward settlement next. Organizations that sell into a buyer market are not, and their public position is a reasonable proxy for how contested the March trial date remains.

CEO Summary
Fox CEO Lachlan Murdoch told investors this month that Fox will hold its current NFL deal and pricing through the 2029 season rather than renegotiate early. U.S. broadcasters will spend roughly $36.5 billion on sports rights in 2026, up 75% from $20.8 billion in 2021.
Why This Matters
Two analysts on the record connect the sports bill to everything else a network buys. Sam Nursall of Ampere says a broadcaster paying $3 billion a year for the NFL starts passing on cheaper competitions, and Daniel Cohen of Octagon says the same discipline now hits the tech bidders, whose capital is going to AI data centers. That combination undercuts the assumption that Amazon, Google or Netflix will absorb whatever traditional broadcasters drop.
Specific Implication
Fox's entertainment programming budget is protected by its own decision through 2029 and unprotected after it. Sellers with multi-year Fox commitments that extend past that window should price the renewal risk now, while the 2030 opt-out is still four years out.
The Facts
  • Fox Corp. CEO Lachlan Murdoch said on the company's recent earnings call that Fox will keep its existing NFL deal and pricing through the 2029 season rather than renegotiate early. Murdoch said Fox had held "thorough and productive discussions" with the league before deciding against amending the agreement.
  • Fox's NFL agreement runs through 2033. The NFL holds a one-time right to terminate after the 2029 season, covering 2030 through 2033.
  • Based on the roughly 50% increase the NFL has reportedly sought in other rights talks, a similar jump would add about $1.1 billion per year to Fox's NFL spending, according to Ampere.
  • Ampere estimates Fox will spend roughly $7 billion on all content in 2026, including about $4 billion on sports. Another $1.1 billion for the NFL alone would be roughly a 15% increase in total content spending.
  • Fox pays roughly $2.03 billion annually in NFL rights fees, according to Octagon Media Rights Consulting, which estimates the package is around break-even to slightly profitable on a direct basis after amortizing the advertising lift from Super Bowl broadcasts.
  • U.S. broadcasters will spend roughly $36.5 billion on sports rights in 2026, per Ampere, up 75% from about $20.8 billion in 2021.
  • Annual NFL rights fees rose from roughly $7.7 billion in 2022-23 to $12.4 billion in 2023-24. The NBA's new agreements took its annual rights haul from $2.7 billion to $6.8 billion beginning with the 2025-26 season.
  • "If a broadcaster has to pay $3 billion annually for the NFL, they might tend to pass on less expensive competitions," Ampere analyst Sam Nursall told TheWrap. "I'm hard-pressed to imagine a world where Fox does not have NFL rights."
  • "The NFL is a need-to-have for many, and a want-to-have for all," said Daniel Cohen, EVP of Octagon Media Rights Consulting. Cohen also said AI spending is a competing priority for tech bidders: "Spending discipline is hitting the tech giants in a big way and Fox knows this."
  • Nursall pointed to Versant's post-NBC spinoff sports strategy, which has taken rights to the new Pac-12, the WNBA, League One Volleyball and Bundesliga, as an example of opportunities opening for midsized buyers.
  • Fox Sports declined to comment beyond the company's earnings remarks.

Apple Music Is Making AI Disclosure Mandatory, and a Third of Its New Uploads Are AI-Generated
Apple Music told partners it will require AI Transparency Tags on any content where AI created a material portion. Apple head Oliver Schusser has said over a third of new monthly uploads are AI-generated.
CEO Summary
Apple Music told industry partners in an email obtained by The Hollywood Reporter that AI labels will launch later this year and that content providers will be required to tag any content where AI created a material portion. The company gave no launch date and no enforcement detail. Apple Music does not detect AI content itself and relies on labels and distributors to declare it. Spotify announced its own AI-artist labeling earlier in August.
Why This Matters
Apple put the duty on the supplier and kept none of it. Apple detects nothing, so whoever signs the declaration carries the exposure if the declaration turns out to be wrong, and the trigger phrase, "a material portion of the content," goes undefined in the announcement.

Apple and Spotify also chose different objects to label. Apple tags the work. Spotify tags the artist profile and excludes those profiles from editorial and algorithmic recommendation, which is a distribution penalty rather than a disclosure. The gap between a labeling regime and a demotion regime is where platform AI policy will actually be contested.
Specific Implication
A supplier-side AI declaration is now a live delivery requirement in one medium and transfers directly to film and television delivery schedules. Anyone likely to be asked to sign one should establish now who inside a production actually knows what tools were used.
The Facts
  • Apple Music told industry partners in an email on Thursday, August 20, obtained by The Hollywood Reporter, that it will launch labels on AI-created songs "later this year." No specific launch date was given.
  • The email states: "Content providers will be required to include AI Transparency Tags in any instance where AI was used to create a material portion of the content, including tracks that are AI platform generated." Apple defines AI-platform-generated content as "anything that is primarily derived from a generative AI service."
  • Apple Music launched Transparency Tags in March for labels and distributors to voluntarily disclose content "materially generated using AI." The upcoming change makes the tags visible and mandatory.
  • Apple Music did not include details on how the requirement will be enforced.
  • Apple Music does not detect AI content itself; it relies on labels and distributors to declare it.
  • The announcement follows an RIAA and IFPI-led initiative calling on streaming services to add AI labels in a manner similar to explicit-content disclosure.
  • Spotify said earlier in August it will label AI artists and exclude them from editorial and algorithmic recommendations. Spotify's labeling attaches to artist profiles, not individual songs. Its April song-level labeling feature is voluntary; Spotify says it sees tens of thousands of credits submitted daily.
  • Apple Music doubled its penalty fees for streaming fraud in January, with Apple Music head Oliver Schusser citing the proliferation of AI content as a factor.
  • Schusser subsequently told Billboard that over a third of Apple Music's new monthly uploads were AI-generated songs, while actual usage of AI songs was less than 1 percent.

'Hadestown' Grossed $20.7 Million as a Filmed Stage Show and Drove Broadway Ticket Sales Up Instead of Down
Bleecker Street's West End capture took $20.7 million, past "Hamilton" at just under $17 million, on a five-night event dated July 24 between "The Odyssey" and "Spider-Man."
CEO Summary
"Hadestown: The Musical," a filmed capture of the West End production released by Bleecker Street's Crosswalk label, has grossed $20.7 million, making it the highest-grossing live theater capture and passing "Hamilton," which took just under $17 million domestically in 2025. Billed as a five-night event, the run extended four weeks. It goes on demand August 25 and to physical media October 20.
Why This Matters
Only one of the two claims here is proven. Bleecker Street can document the gross. The cannibalization answer comes from the show's own creative producer describing what she observed, and the fear it addresses has kept a lot of running shows off screens.

The reporting does establish a repeatable mechanic: tickets on sale six weeks out, trailer released the same day, scarcity in the messaging, and a date in the one open week between two of the year's biggest films.

Sanderson adds the part that outlasts this title. A theatrical run made buyers willing to pay for the disc later, which argues for the window on grounds other than box office.
Specific Implication
For a rights holder with a stage property, the capture is a separate revenue line with its own theatrical, transactional and physical windows. Bundling it into a streaming deal as a promotional asset gives away three of them.
The Facts
  • "Hadestown: The Musical," a filmed capture of the West End production, has grossed $20.7 million, making it the highest-grossing live theater capture ever. It surpasses "Hamilton," which took just under $17 million domestically when released theatrically in 2025 after a long run on Disney+.
  • Billed as a "five night only" event, the run was extended for four weeks on demand.
  • Bleecker Street released it through Crosswalk, a division the company launched in 2025 for "event cinema." Crosswalk has also distributed "Waitress: The Musical" and "Stray Kids: The dominate Experience," a concert film from SoFi Stadium. "George Michael: The Faith Tour" is next.
  • Bleecker Street CEO Kent Sanderson on the campaign: "We put tickets on sale about six weeks before the film actually came out, and released the trailer on the same day with messaging to go buy tickets now because it will only be in theaters for a few nights."
  • It opened July 24, 2026, between "The Odyssey" (July 17) and "Spider-Man: Brand New Day" (July 31). Sanderson: "People probably thought we were crazy to go between two record-breaking movies. But we found our lane and were able to create the room we needed to coexist."
  • Three performances were captured at London's Lyric Theatre by Steam Motion and Sound.
  • The film goes on demand August 25; DVD and Blu-ray follow October 20. Sanderson said that within a couple of hours of pre-sales opening it was the number three physical media product on Amazon.
  • Sanderson on why the theatrical run raises downstream value: "releasing it in theaters makes it a more premium experience and that allows people to justify renting or buying the film later in a way they wouldn't if it were a straight-to-streaming release."
  • Creative producer Mara Isaacs said the stage productions saw a surge in ticket sales after the film's release, as did streams of the Broadway cast recording. Some theater producers have resisted filming shows still running on Broadway and the West End for fear cheaper access would suppress live ticket sales.
  • "Hadestown" originated as a concept album by Anaïs Mitchell, was developed in regional workshops and off-Broadway with director Rachel Chavkin, opened on Broadway in 2019 and won the Tony for best musical.

Netflix Made Its First Co-Production Deal With a Traditional Studio and Takes Second Position at Home
AMC Studios is lead studio on Shane Black's Bannerman. AMC premieres it in the U.S. and Canada, and Netflix gets it there 90 days after the season finale airs.
CEO Summary
Netflix has agreed with AMC Studios to jointly develop and produce original series, believed to be the first co-production arrangement of its kind for the streamer. The first greenlight is Bannerman, a drama from Shane Black and Craig Silverstein based on John R. Maxim's spy novels. AMC Studios leads. Netflix carries the show exclusively outside the U.S., Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Spain, and waits 90 days past the AMC finale for U.S. and Canadian rights.
Why This Matters
Netflix has spent a decade refusing to premiere behind another outlet at home. Here it accepted a 90-day wait behind a cable network in the U.S. and Canada and bought exclusivity everywhere else in exchange. AMC Studios holds the lead-studio position, so Netflix is funding and sharing a series it does not control.
Specific Implication
A seller who wants a domestic linear premiere alongside Netflix's international reach now has a precedent to point at, with the lead-studio position and the length of the domestic gap as the negotiable terms.
The Facts
  • Netflix has made a deal with AMC Studios to jointly develop and produce original series, believed to be the first of its kind for Netflix.
  • The first greenlight is Bannerman, from Shane Black and Craig Silverstein, based on the spy novels by John R. Maxim. The series spans five books.
  • Black co-wrote the first episode and will executive produce and direct the first two, his first TV series. Silverstein will showrun, write and executive produce, retaining his EP credit on Disney+'s Percy Jackson and the Olympians. Greg Nicotero and Brian Witten also executive produce.
  • AMC Studios is lead studio. Bannerman premieres on AMC in the U.S. and Canada and reaches Netflix there 90 days after the season finale airs.
  • Netflix and AMC will jointly debut each episode in Australia, New Zealand and Spain. Netflix carries the show exclusively everywhere else.
  • Dan McDermott, chief content officer of AMC Global Media and president of AMC Studios: "This is the perfect premium drama to kick off our first co-production with Netflix, and we are thrilled to continue evolving and expanding our partnership by jointly developing and producing select original series for our respective platforms."
  • Deadline frames the deal as opening "a new avenue for Netflix to collaborate with traditional studios," following the co-licensing model introduced roughly a decade ago by now-Netflix Chief Content Officer Bela Bajaria.
  • The relationship dates to Breaking Bad becoming Netflix's first hit. Earlier this month the two announced a $500 million licensing deal for the entire The Walking Dead universe. Netflix also recently took AMC Studios' drama The Headlands House, starring Colman Domingo, into development.
  • Netflix's series team includes former AMC scripted executives Emma Miller and Carrie Gillogly, who moved three years ago.
  • AMC Studios acquired the Bannerman rights in January 2023 and opened a writers room at AMC Global Media's 2026 upfront.

Paramount's Former Distribution Chief Says He Was Fired Two Months Into a Contract Running to 2028
Chris Aronson signed the deal in July and was terminated without cause on September 29. His complaint puts the unpaid salary and incentive compensation at roughly $3.9 million.
CEO Summary
Chris Aronson, former domestic distribution chief at Paramount Pictures, has sued the studio over compensation he says he is owed after being let go in layoffs that followed the Skydance merger. His attorney filed the complaint in Los Angeles County Superior Court on August 20. Aronson puts total projected economic damages above $4 million. The complaint also alleges age discrimination, citing layoff data showing 62 employees aged 40 or older were let go against 30 under 40. Paramount declined comment.
Why This Matters
The contract permitted termination without cause, so the dispute is about what the payout provision obligated. Aronson's complaint quotes co-chair Josh Greenstein assuring him Paramount would "pay you everything you're owed under your contract." Assurances given in a termination meeting are enforceable only where the agreement already says so.
Specific Implication
An executive papering a deal with a studio in the middle of an integration should confirm that the pay-on-termination obligation is a stated term of the agreement rather than a discretionary practice.
The Facts
  • Aronson was terminated on September 29 of last year, roughly two months into a contract signed in July that would have kept him at Paramount until December 1, 2028.
  • Attorney Barry Kaufman told THR he filed the complaint with Superior Court of Los Angeles County on August 20; it had not been formally processed before the document leaked online. Kaufman: "I have not even received back a conformed copy of the Complaint and the associated documents from the court confirming that it was accepted for filing."
  • Per the complaint, Aronson was summoned to a meeting with new Paramount co-chairs Dana Goldberg and Josh Greenstein, who told him he was terminated "without cause." Greenstein assured him Paramount would "pay you everything you're owed under your contract" and "added words to the effect that 'you're worth every penny.'"
  • Aronson was told Paramount intended to "downgrade the position" he occupied.
  • The complaint: "the remaining salary and incentive compensation under the agreement had an estimate value approaching $3.9 million." With lost benefits and related components, "Aronson's projected economic damages exceed $4 million."
  • Aronson was 69 at the time. His complaint cites disclosure data on the broader layoffs plus an independently commissioned analysis finding a statistical pattern of age discrimination: 62 employees aged 40 or older laid off against 30 staffers under 40.
  • Paramount hired Shaun Barber, 18 years at Lionsgate and Summit, as domestic distribution chief in November. Aronson stayed until December 1, when Barber took over.
  • Aronson oversaw theatrical distribution on Top Gun: Maverick and multiple Mission: Impossible, Sonic the Hedgehog and A Quiet Place titles. He joined Paramount in 2019 after running distribution at 20th Century Fox, and his contract was renewed in 2022 and again in 2025.
  • Paramount executives "suggested and dangled the prospect of a future consulting relationship" that never materialized. Aronson later took a consulting role at Rentrak Theatrical, formerly Comscore Movies, a division he founded.
  • Paramount declined comment on the suit.

Three Companies Take 94 Percent of a $150 Billion Vertical Video Market

CEO Summary
Vertical media is projected to generate $150 billion in revenue in 2026 outside China, a 42 percent gain over 2025, according to Owl & Co.'s first-half report. The U.S. accounts for about 40 percent of that. Meta, ByteDance and YouTube together generate 94 percent of the total. Owl & Co. counts nearly 2,000 apps worldwide competing for the remainder, with vertical-app startups including ReelShort, DramaBox, PineDrama and MyDrama spending heavily on customer acquisition.
Why This Matters
New series launches rose 25 percent in the second quarter while total watch time for new series fell 4 percent, which is the oversupply curve subscription streaming took a decade to reach.

The Facts
  • Vertical media is projected to generate $150 billion in revenue in 2026 in global markets outside China, a 42% gain over 2025, per Owl & Co.'s "Vertical Economy Report 1H26: Mapping Consumption, Creation, Value Capture Across a $150B Audiovisual Language."
  • Hernan Lopez, founder and CEO of Owl & Co., is the report's author.
  • $131 billion of the total is expected to come from advertising via platforms including TikTok, Instagram, YouTube and Facebook. Variety notes the numbers are approaching the volume of revenue generated in the U.S. by subscription streaming platforms.
  • Meta (Instagram, Facebook), ByteDance (TikTok) and YouTube generate 94% of the $150 billion. Meta draws 27% of its total revenue from vertical media, YouTube 22%, ByteDance 72%.
  • The U.S. accounts for about 40% of the projected 2026 revenue.
  • Owl & Co. counts nearly 2,000 apps worldwide fielding content. New series introductions grew 25% in the second quarter while total watch time of new series declined 4%.
  • Lopez writes: "Traditional streaming learned years ago about the diminishing marginal returns of launching too many shows."
  • On customer acquisition: "Some creators and show producers are finding viewership organically. But the apps themselves are spending a significant share of their revenue in customer acquisition. It's a lot like what TikTok was doing in the year 2020 when it was becoming popular."
  • Lopez on studio participation: "I think it makes sense for every company to lean into this medium which really represents a new native-digital visual language. Disney has a brand that's so unique and it has a global fandom. It makes it obvious why they will be the first ones to do it, but I think the one step that nobody has taken at scale is to produce original verticals."
  • Romance and drama thriller remain the dominant genres. Business, finance and news programs accounted for 12% of vertical media views outside China.

Charter closed the $34.5 billion Cox merger and John Malone exited Charter entirely
Liberty Broadband's 27 percent stake, held since 2013, is gone, and two Malone-designated directors left the board. The parent company will take the Cox Communications name.
CEO Summary
Charter Communications closed its $34.5 billion acquisition of Cox Communications on Thursday, creating a cable and broadband operator serving roughly 37 million customers across 45 states. The California Public Utility Commission granted the final regulatory clearance last week. Within a year the parent company will be renamed Cox Communications, while services continue to sell under the Spectrum brand. Chris Winfrey stays on as president and CEO. Alex Taylor, previously chairman and CEO of Cox Enterprises, becomes chairman of the combined company.
Why This Matters
Malone put 27 percent into Charter in 2013 and walks away owning none of it. He built the modern American cable roll-up and has cashed out of it at the point where the distribution business has consolidated about as far as regulators will allow. Charter took Time Warner Cable and Bright House for $67.1 billion in 2016. Comcast's $45.2 billion run at Time Warner Cable died under Obama-era pushback. Cox was the last comparable independent left to buy.
Specific Implication
Programmers negotiating carriage in former Cox markets now face Spectrum where they previously faced a separate counterparty. Renewal leverage in those markets moves toward the distributor.
The Facts
  • Deal value $34.5 billion, announced May 2025, closed Aug. 20, 2026.
  • Roughly 37 million customers across 45 states (Variety). Deadline reported 38 million subscribers to video, internet and wireless.
  • CPUC approval last week was the final federal or state clearance required.
  • Headquarters stays in Stamford, Conn., with a "significant presence" retained near Atlanta.

A secret three-year AI group run by Kathleen Kennedy and AFI published its first framework
The group's document sorts AI use into three tiers and attaches a copyright status to each, calling purely prompted performances, voices and stories not copyrightable.
CEO Summary
Producer Kathleen Kennedy and American Film Institute dean Susan Ruskin have convened Oscar-winning filmmakers, actors, studio executives and Silicon Valley figures in private since November 2023. The Ankler, which attended off the record, published the group's first public document on Thursday. It proposes three categories of AI use in final footage: utility and embedded tools, Human Generative Workflows, and Machine Generative. The first two are described as copyrightable; the third is not. The group calls it an argument, not a standard.
Why This Matters
The tiers borrow their authority from the U.S. Copyright Office rather than from any body that could enforce them. That is what makes them usable: a production adopting the vocabulary is describing its chain of title, not making a marketing claim, which is why the language will show up in AI riders before it shows up in any formal standard.

The document also names what it declined to settle: training data, licensing, consent, labor transition, economic policy. Those carry the money.
Specific Implication
Anyone drafting an AI provision now has a published definition to point at instead of building one per deal. The tier a use falls into determines whether the output is claimed as copyrightable, which is a term worth specifying.
The Facts
  • The meetings began at artist Refik Anadol's Los Angeles studio in November 2023, weeks after the strikes ended, then moved to the AFI campus. Google VP of technology and society Mira Lane on the choice of venue: AFI "has all the heads of the big studios, all the guilds are part of the board of trustees."
  • Last weekend the group expanded to roughly 120 participants for sessions on authorship, standards, transparency and control.
  • The three tiers: Utility Techniques and Embedded AI (denoising, upscaling, rotoscoping, markerless mocap, wire removal), described as copyrightable. Human Generative Workflows (artist-controlled pipelines in Nuke, Unreal, Blender, ComfyUI and DaVinci Resolve using narrowly trained LoRA models and structured inputs), described as copyrightable. Machine Generative (purely prompted likenesses, voices, performances or stories), described as not copyrightable.
  • The document quotes U.S. Copyright Office guidance that "prompts do not alone provide sufficient control," and that protection extends only to human contributions.
  • Worked example: "Dear Upstairs Neighbors," a six-minute animated short directed by Connie He, produced by Marcia Mayer, made by roughly 45 people including Pixar and DreamWorks veterans with Google DeepMind engineers. It premiered at Tribeca in June 2026.
  • Jon Avnet, DGA AI Committee co-chair with Christopher Nolan, led a weekend panel: "The key thing was to start the conversation in light of day."
  • The document cites existing market positions: A24's "Heretic" (2024) credited "No generative AI was used in the making of this film"; Vince Gilligan's "Pluribus" (2025) closed "This show was made by humans"; DreamWorks' "Bad Guys 2" used credits to prohibit AI training on the work.
  • Proposed next steps: publish the vocabulary for response, open consent talks on machine-generative outputs of actors, engage with certification efforts, and extend to music, sound and the writing room.

Spanish novelist Mercedes Ron signed a first-look deal with Amazon MGM Studios in June 2026 covering executive producer credit on all current and future adaptations of her work, plus the right to bring other authors to the studio as an EP. Eleven of her books are in adaptation at Prime Video. The 2023 adaptation of "Culpa Mía" was the biggest non-English-language original launch in Prime Video history; the three Spanish-language Culpables films have drawn more than 100 million viewers, over 90 percent from outside Spain.
Why This Matters
Amazon bought volume certainty from an author with a measured audience and paid in credit and consultation, not control.

Ron reads scripts, comments on casting and gives notes on cuts, and says outright that she is not the one saying no. She also has no access to the platform's numbers on her own films, so at renewal the studio can price her and she cannot price herself. Asked whether her June agreement sets any limit on generative use of her characters, she said she did not think so, then said she would call her agent.
Specific Implication
A rights holder signing a catalogue-level adaptation deal should treat performance-data access and AI-use parameters as terms to request, not defaults.
The Facts
  • Ron, 33, has sold more than 6 million books in 26 languages. Her Culpables trilogy has more than 80 million reads on Wattpad, where she first posted it chapter by chapter in 2015.
  • "Culpa Mía" (My Fault) reached No. 1 worldwide in its first weekend in 2023. Amazon has not released viewership figures. An English-language remake, "My Fault: London," was greenlit before the Spanish-language films wrapped.
  • She is building a label inside Prime Video called House of Ron. Amazon international originals boss Nicole Clemens has called her the "secret sauce" behind the streamer's YA run, which also includes "The Summer I Turned Pretty," "Off Campus," "We Were Liars," "Maxton Hall" and "Sterling Point."
  • On compensation structure: "As an author and also as a producer. They're separate."
  • On approval rights: "I'm not going to be the one saying 'no' to this or that." She reads scripts, sends comments, and gives notes on cuts.
  • On data: "Prime Video don't share a lot of data. So, no, I don't have all that. I don't have access to that."
  • On genre economics: "For romance, 90 percent of the audience is female, and we know that what women like is always underestimated." She says international YA originals remain underfunded relative to other genres.
  • Her novel "30 Sunsets to Fall in Love" skips a Spanish-language adaptation and goes to the Amazon MGM U.S. team: "this story needs a bigger budget than we can get in the Spanish world."
  • Asked what she would change about her first book deal, she named royalties, and said publishers "want to take advantage of you not knowing anything."
  • Culpables book four is the one title not greenlit.

Why This Matters
Behavioral remedies are conduct promises: release counts, window lengths, in-state production floors, job guarantees. Every commitment Paramount has made publicly falls in that category. Bonta's stated condition therefore does not describe a narrower version of the announced transaction. It describes a different one, in which Warner Bros. assets are sold to a third party before any close.

That position held through a week in which three industry groups moved toward settlement. The DGA and IATSE wrote asking for talks, and Cinema United reversed its opposition. A buyer or financier evaluating Warner Bros. assets should treat a pre-trial divestiture package as a live possibility before the March trial date, not only as a post-verdict outcome.

The load-bearing figure in the report is not the job count. It is roughly $6.7 billion in identified annual cost reductions across overlapping operations, which CVL and the county tie to management's stated goal of reaching investment-grade leverage metrics within three years. That framing turns the job losses from a discretionary corporate choice into a financing requirement. The report adds that if revenues underperform or savings prove harder to reach, pressure for further reductions increases.

The creators holding exclusive deals across the two companies are the population whose paper converts first if development shrinks. Anyone holding one should establish which of the two entities their agreement actually sits with, and what a change of control does to it.

CEO Summary
ABC filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the Federal Communications Commission on Tuesday, arguing that the agency's investigations and regulatory orders were part of a Trump administration effort to punish the network for its coverage. The suit asks the court for a temporary restraining order barring the FCC from further action in the early renewal proceedings. An FCC spokesperson said all broadcasters have a legal obligation to operate in the public interest and that the commission has been examining claims of illegal DEI discrimination at Disney for over a year.
Why This Matters
The hard element in any retaliation claim is causation, and this complaint is built to prove it with the regulator's own words rather than with timing and inference. It quotes Chairman Brendan Carr telling the network's stations "we can do this the easy way or the hard way." It cites his warning that stations airing "fake news" had "a chance now to correct course before their license renewals come up." Most directly, it records Carr stating that the commission would weigh ABC's decision not to carry a July 16 presidential address when reviewing the stations' renewal applications.

The filing also puts the network's own editorial judgment into evidence. ABC's lawyers wrote that it returned Kimmel to air with full awareness that doing so was likely to invite further reprisal. Framing a business decision as a knowingly accepted cost is unusual in a regulatory dispute, and it is what turns an abstract chilling-effect argument into a documented one.
Specific Implication
Broadcast station buyers and affiliate groups now have a live instance of renewal timing used as leverage on licenses that still had two years to run. That belongs in transaction diligence and affiliation negotiations as a priced item rather than a routine administrative step.
The Facts
  • The FCC tied the early renewal order to an ongoing investigation of the network's diversity, equity and inclusion practices.

The pattern inside the ledger is narrower than the year's headline. "Lee Cronin's The Mummy" returned $90 million on a $22 million budget and "Evil Dead Burn" returned $71 million on $20 million. Both are cheap New Line horror. Between $80 million and $180 million, the studio has four consecutive losses, including "Supergirl" at $126 million worldwide against a $180 million budget.

A studio coming off a year like this normally corrects by committing capital to an aggressive development cycle. Warner cannot do that while the Paramount acquisition is contested. The correction available to a company being bought is a freeze, and a 2027 slate assembled entirely from pre-sold franchises is what that looks like on paper.

A filmmaker taking an original, non-franchise feature to Warner Bros. in the next six months should expect the budget conversation to anchor near the New Line horror band rather than near the studio's 2025 comparables.

Why This Matters
The gap between the two figures is the finding. Existing market estimates size microdrama and treat it as the category. On this measure the thing being discussed as an emerging content format is, in revenue terms, principally an advertising business operated by three companies, and the content-shaped portion of it is a rounding error against the whole.

The microdrama segment is also moving away from the model it was built on. Free ad-supported apps went from 15% of time spent to 83% over five quarters. Series releases across the seven leading paid apps rose more than fivefold since the second quarter of this year, while average time spent per new title fell. The report attributes the release volume to widespread use of AI in production.
Specific Implication
A producer entering microdrama is entering a segment whose payment model changed inside five quarters. Terms keyed to in-app purchase revenue share are being written against a shrinking portion of the segment's income.
The Facts
  • Owl & Co was founded by Hernan Lopez, previously founder of Wondery and CEO of Fox International Channels. The firm calls vertical "the third audiovisual language."
  • The report claims to be the first sizing vertical video as a whole rather than as a collection of apps.
  • Microdrama grew from $3 billion in 2025 to a projected $4 billion this year.
  • Lopez: "Vertical is no longer optional. As multiple audience cohorts shift time spent and frequency to vertical, revenue, talent and IP are following."
  • The findings draw on Owl & Co's Vertical Index, which tracks more than 37,000 titles across 14 app libraries and updates daily.

The complaint does not date the injury to the film's 2025 release. That is the load-bearing claim, and it locates the exposure in the franchise extensions rather than in the title. Any rights grant giving a platform downstream music, merchandise and live-event rights on a titled property should be cleared against those categories rather than the film's alone, and the agreement should name which party carries naming-risk indemnity.

Anti-piracy provisions are written against unauthorized copying by third parties. Theatrical exclusivity covenants bind the distributor. This incident was neither. CEO Summary
ABC filed a First Amendment lawsuit against the FCC on Tuesday in federal court in Washington, D.C., naming the agency, chairman Brendan Carr and both commissioners. It seeks a temporary restraining order to halt the proceeding requiring ABC's eight owned stations to seek early license renewal, plus an order barring the FCC from acting to coerce the network over editorial decisions. No network had previously sued the agency.
Why This Matters
The complaint's central argument is procedural, and that is what makes it unusual. ABC is not asking a court to declare the FCC's motives unlawful in the abstract. It argues that the agency cannot lawfully grant an early renewal at all, which means every available outcome inside the FCC process is adverse, and the only remaining question is whether the harm arrives as years of litigation or as revocation. On that reading, participating in the agency proceeding is itself the loss, which is why the relief sought is an injunction against the proceeding rather than a ruling on the merits.

Timing supports the urgency claim. Bloomberg reported the FCC may issue a hearing designation order this month, which would open the adjudication ABC is trying to prevent.
Specific Implication
Owned-station groups now have a documented case that an early-renewal proceeding, on its own, constitutes the injury. Broadcasters facing similar FCC action have a filed template for seeking injunctive relief before a hearing designation order issues rather than after.
The Facts
  • The suit names the FCC, Carr, and commissioners Olivia Trusty and Anna Gomez, and was filed in federal court in Washington, D.C.
  • From the complaint: "Acting through the Federal Communications Commission, the Administration has waged a retaliatory campaign against ABC for a single reason: it disapproves of what ABC broadcasts."
  • ABC on the range of outcomes: the FCC may "intentionally prolong the adjudicative process, miring ABC in years of costly litigation," or "use the hearing to deny license renewal or immediately revoke the Stations' licenses."
  • The first of the eight station licenses was not due for renewal until 2028.
  • The FCC cited an investigation of The Walt Disney Co.'s DEI policies when ordering early renewals. ABC calls it "pretextual," saying cooperation "simply begat increasingly aggressive demands."
  • The complaint cites Carr's September podcast remark, after a Jimmy Kimmel joke tied to the Charlie Kirk assassination investigation, that "we can do this the easy way or the hard way." Two station groups declined to air the show and ABC pulled Kimmel for several days.

CEO Summary
Three individuals with knowledge of the deal told TheWrap that Tom Holland took a base salary of at least $20 million on "Spider-Man: Brand New Day," up $10 million from "No Way Home," with an uncapped backend bonus that one source said will pay him at least $100 million. The term that distinguishes this deal is the absence of a ceiling, not the size of the guarantee. An uncapped escalator converts the studio's exposure into a variable that only grows when the studio is already winning, which is how it clears business affairs when a raised guarantee would not.

Contract expiry is what created the opening. Holland's six-picture deal ended with "No Way Home," so the negotiation started from zero on a dated release with no substitute performer available.

Performers reaching the end of an option ladder on a proven franchise should treat the expiry itself as the leverage event, and should press for an uncapped escalator rather than a larger fixed guarantee, since the studio prices the two differently.

Netflix Outspent The MPA In Washington For The First Time In 2025
Netflix spent $3.1 million lobbying Washington in 2025 against the MPA's $2.7 million, while also paying the MPA roughly $10 million a year in dues.
CEO Summary
Stephen Follows compiled every federal lobbying disclosure filed by the major Hollywood players since 1999: 3,437 filings containing 8,218 individual items through June 2026. In 2025 Netflix outspent the Motion Picture Association for the first time, $3.1 million to $2.7 million. Netflix's top lobbying subject is telecommunications, not copyright, which has been the MPA's number-one subject in 19 of the past 27 years. The dataset also dates the arrival of AI as a lobbying issue to the quarter ChatGPT launched.
Why This Matters
The studio side files roughly twice the AI lobbying volume of the guilds: 48 items to 22 in 2025, and 32 to 14 in the first half of 2026. Both camps publicly support the No Fakes Act, which cleared Senate Judiciary unanimously in June, and Follows notes that the two sides "do not want the same thing" on the underlying question of building with AI versus protecting against it.

That volume gap matters because statutory language is where the ambiguity gets resolved. A likeness right established by federal statute becomes the floor beneath every digital-replica clause currently negotiated deal by deal, and the party filing twice as often is the party in the room more often while the text is drafted.
Specific Implication
Performers and their counsel negotiating digital-replica terms should not assume the No Fakes Act will settle the question in their favor by default. The provision-level drafting is being shaped in a forum where the studio side is filing at roughly twice the guilds' volume.
The Facts
  • Dataset: 3,437 federal lobbying filings containing 8,218 individual items, covering the MPA, Netflix, Paramount, the other legacy studios, the cinema chains and the major guilds since 1999, through June 2026.
  • 2024: MPA $3.1 million, Netflix $1.9 million. 2025: Netflix $3.1 million, MPA $2.7 million. First time a single filmed-entertainment company outspent the trade body.
  • Netflix pays the MPA roughly $10 million a year in dues, judging by MPA tax filings. The MPA does not disclose the figure.
  • H1 2026: Netflix $2.15 million, $1.28 million in Q1 alone, while pursuing Warner Bros. Discovery's studio and streaming division. On pace to break its own record.
  • Netflix outside firms: three in 2024, six in 2025, nine in H1 2026. It hired Ballard Partners, whose quarterly Netflix retainer nearly doubled to $150,000 at the start of 2026. Paramount also retained Ballard during the bidding war.
  • Netflix's bid failed after Paramount pledged $31 a share for the whole company.
  • Paramount's in-house lobbying hit $6.2 million in 2025, its highest in 27 years of filings; $2.9 million in H1 2026. Figures cover the whole company including CBS News.
  • Netflix's top subjects are telecommunications, then communications and broadcasting. Its own disclosures rank "content delivery" first and "intellectual property protection" second. It funds Incompas and, since 2024, the Alliance for the Open Internet.
  • Copyright has been the MPA's top subject in 19 of 27 years and every year since 2018. Total MPA lobbying spend since 1999: $59.2 million.
  • Disney's top subject across 490 items since 1999 is broadcasting at nearly four in 10, with tax second and copyright third at about one in 10. Alone among the studios its top subjects include travel and tourism.
  • Federal tax was a fifth or more of MPA lobbying in the early 2000s, fell below a tenth by the early 2020s, and is back at 17% in 2025 and 19% in H1 2026. Recent entries name the CREATE Act and the Section 181 film deduction.
  • Trade peaked at 26% of MPA lobbying in 2019 and is at 14% in H1 2026. China mentions peaked 2019 to 2021.
  • AI first appears in Q4 2022, the quarter ChatGPT launched, on a bill criminalizing faked explicit images. Zero mentions ever before that. Both quarters of 2026 hit 23 items, the highest on record.
  • Of 215 AI items, the MPA's own team accounts for 41; Paramount, the DGA and Sony Pictures are the next largest in-house voices. Busiest outside firm on AI is the Goodlatte Group.
  • Comcast, Apple and Amazon are excluded from film-industry totals because a filing reports one figure across all topics.

California will exempt indie film credits from its $5 million tax cap but not studio credits
Independent film credits are transferable and can be sold to buyers offsetting state tax. Studio credits are not, and the deal gives studios only faster refunds inside the cap.
CEO Summary
California lawmakers are close to a deal easing the effect of Senate Bill 122, the June budget measure that caps annual corporate tax credits at 70 percent of liability or $5 million, whichever is greater, for three years. Per Variety's sources, the agreement would exempt independent film production credits outright while creating a mechanism to accelerate refunds on studio projects, and would extend the expiration date on old non-refundable credits by five years. Lawmakers face an August 31 deadline to pass bills this session.
Why This Matters
The split follows the instrument, not the industry. An indie credit is collateral: it is sold to a third party and banked before a frame is shot, so a cap on the buyer's annual claim destroys its value at the moment of financing. A studio credit is an accounting entry against a large liability, and delay costs interest rather than access to capital. Lawmakers protected the financeable one.

The Entertainment Union Coalition memo makes the financing point directly, warning the cap would make it harder for independent productions "to sell their tax credits to buyers or even get financing from banks."
Specific Implication
Producers financing California independents can continue to price a transferable state credit into the capital stack. Studio-side budgets shot in California should model the credit as a multi-year receivable rather than a near-term offset when comparing against New York, Illinois, Canada or the United Kingdom.
The Facts
  • Gov. Gavin Newsom signed SB 122 on June 29 as part of the budget package. The cap was written to stop companies, particularly in tech, from erasing state tax liability through research and development credits.
  • The legislative fix is led by Assemblyman Rick Chavez Zbur and Sen. Ben Allen, who had sought a full carveout. Newsom's office is in the negotiations; the Office of Business and Economic Development declined to comment.
  • The cap lands one year after California raised its production incentive from $330 million to $750 million, a program that has qualified more than 110 film, television and animation projects.
  • The Entertainment Union Coalition says more than 350,000 letters have been sent by union members to Sacramento lawmakers over SB 122.
  • ProdPro reported a 5 percent year-over-year rise in California production spending last quarter.
  • Lawmakers have been mindful that a full film carveout would prompt tech companies to demand one of their own.
  • A separate bill, AB 2319, would create a 35 to 50 percent refundable credit for post-production work. A $150 million soundstage-construction incentive has been fully depleted; reauthorization is expected next session.
  • One person involved told Variety: "There was a lot of fanfare over the expansion. It feels like there was a commitment that was made and that was rescinded."
  • Zbur told TheWrap: "we are in the process of building out a fix that would mitigate the impacts that SB 122 has on this program."

Higgsfield Published The Prompts Behind Its Cannes AI Feature And Made Certification Free
Higgsfield's CEO says the $100 million exclusive contracts other AI companies pitched to studios "completely overpromised and underdelivered," so his company is giving its prompts away instead.
CEO Summary
Higgsfield AI launched Higgsfield Academy in August, publishing the prompts used to make "Hell Grind," its 95-minute AI-generated feature that premiered at the Marché du Film at Cannes in May, and offering free certification in its Cinema Studio platform. The company reports a $500 million annual run rate reached within 14 months, over 26 million users, and use by 390 of the Fortune 500. Co-founder and CEO Mahi de Silva said the company is "not in the content creation business" but "in the tools distribution business."
Why This Matters
De Silva stated the switching cost on the record: "You can cut and paste a prompt right out of our system and play it somewhere else, but you're likely not to get the visual coherence, the visual fidelity from scene to scene. That's part of our magic." Publishing the prompts is therefore not a giveaway of the product. It distributes the part that ports and retains the part that does not, while building a pool of filmmakers trained on one company's workflow.

The likeness detail sits underneath. Higgsfield's second feature, "The Cully Hill Boys," used the likenesses of Israel Adesanya, Quinton "Rampage" Jackson and the creator N3on in a film the company describes as a teaching tool rather than content. That is a use case standard digital-replica language was not drafted around.
Specific Implication
Anyone granting likeness rights to an AI platform should establish whether the resulting material will function as a production, a product demonstration, or training data, since those three carry different reuse and duration terms.
The Facts
  • Higgsfield Academy launched in August, publishing the prompts behind "Hell Grind" and offering free platform certification.

  • The company surpassed a $500 million annual run rate within 14 months, claiming to be the fastest-growing generative AI company in history. Higgsfield.ai reports over 31 million monthly visits and over 26 million users.
  • Its platform is used by 390 of the Fortune 500 and more than 170,000 corporate accounts.
  • De Silva on the prior vendor approach: companies told studios "you can sign an exclusive deal with us. You have to commit $100 million to a contract, and trust us, we're going to make it work for you... And I think the companies that did that have completely overpromised and underdelivered."
  • De Silva on positioning: "I think it sends mixed signals to studios if they think we're going to try to compete with them... We are not in the content creation business. We're in the tools distribution business."
  • De Silva declined to characterize the company's Hollywood customer base in detail, but said Higgsfield has supported filmmakers on reshoots and visual effects.
  • A single shot's prompt can require instructions covering characters, environments, camera movement, lighting, action and continuity, plus assets already built inside Cinema Studio.
  • Second feature "The Cully Hill Boys" used the likenesses of two-time UFC champion Israel Adesanya, MMA veteran Quinton "Rampage" Jackson and livestream creator N3on.
  • Content lead Adil Alimzhanov on the first Academy lesson, identifying AI artifacts: "The plastic look, where the skin is too smooth, the lighting is too perfect, and then the uncanny valley effect, where everything is too symmetrical, too perfect."

Why This Matters
Export growth and rights ownership are separate measurements, and this study reports both. A sector can post 15.4% annual export growth while 40% of its companies own nothing they ship, which describes work-for-hire volume rather than a rights position.

The screen side shows the same structure one level up. The study's own case study reports that "MasterChef Australia," an adaptation of a British format, generates an estimated AUD700 million a year in licensing and commercial revenue for Banijay, its French-owned rights holder. Endemol Shine Australia COO Scott Howard said on the record that the country's success adapting formats has not been matched by investment in original local IP.
Specific Implication
Buyers and financiers evaluating a production territory should ask for the rights-retention split alongside the output and export figures, since this study shows the two can move in opposite directions inside the same sector.
The Facts

  • Games exports grew 15.4% annually between 2016/17 and 2023/24, versus 4.7% annually for screen exports since 2008/09. Games are roughly a fifth of total sector export earnings.

  • "Bluey" is named the country's most effective cultural export, cited as the most-streamed show in the U.S. in 2025.
  • Audience gap: 84% of Australians rate local screen content as important to access and 75% want more, but only 36% consider it easy to find, and nearly two-thirds watch it for under 30% of total viewing time.
  • Government funding, direct and indirect, is now the leading finance source behind Australian narrative drama, documentary and children's television.

  • Screen Australia CEO Deirdre Brennan said future success depends on "businesses building durable intellectual property, strengthening audience relationships and improving discoverability in a market increasingly shaped by algorithms and platform recommendations rather than active search."

Media Res CEO Michael Ellenberg says the era of $10 million per episode is over
Ellenberg puts the condition plainly: "If you want a big budget, you better be very clear how you're going to hit a wide audience. Otherwise, it's not happening right now."
CEO Summary
Michael Ellenberg, founder and CEO of Media Res and formerly head of drama at HBO, told The Ankler that "the era of $10 [million] and over per episode for almost any show is over" and that budget discipline "has arrived, and it's serious." He said the post-strike period when buyers asked sellers to "bring us the formulas" has ended, with no clear rules replacing it. Media Res is in business with Apple, Netflix, HBO, Hulu, Peacock and 20th Television, and its The Morning Show returns in 2027 for a fifth and final season.
Why This Matters
A stated per-episode ceiling from a seller who sells to every major buyer is a usable comp, and it is rare to get one on the record. Ellenberg pairs it with a trade rather than a complaint: lower budgets buy creative latitude, and he frames the return of that math as healthy, saying "the lower-budget you are, the more freedom you're going to have."

He also names a gap nobody has filled. On the film side he cites Obsession at roughly $1 million and Backrooms at around $10 million as breakthrough successes. In television, he says, "lower-budget TV for the most part has meant mid-tier programming, not radical programming."
Specific Implication
Sellers should canvass every buyer rather than target a presumed natural home. Ellenberg says each buyer's definition of success is amorphous and that "things change monthly at the buyers," with projects passed on by the platform they seemed built for and picked up by one that seemed a long shot.
The Facts
  • Ellenberg on cadence: "Just as important as the total budget is how frequently can you make it? Can you come back faster?" He ties season-to-season audience dropoff to slow returns.
  • On limited series: buyers moved from "Absolutely not. No more limiteds" back to accepting them. "That era feels over as well."
  • On audience behavior: "The audience is frisky and curious and rewarding big swings. Frankly, the things that feel safer right now are harder to break through."
  • On buyer metrics: "They're evaluating how much are you speaking to existing viewers, how much are you converting new viewers, are they finishing the show, how many are sampling the show."
  • His four questions before taking a project: is it noisy, is it castable, is it a big swing, and can you get a buyer excited.
  • On the indie market: "The market is as friendly to the independents as it's been since Media Res started." He names HBO, Apple, FX, Hulu and Netflix as robust programmers, noting Netflix launched a prestige division under Nora Skinner.
  • Media Res slate: The Dealer with Jessica Chastain and Adam Driver at Apple; Durango with 20th Television at Hulu; Enigma Variations with Aaron Taylor-Johnson at Netflix; The Chain with Damon Lindelof and Advantage Player with Will Graham and Riley Keough at HBO; The Miniature Wife at Peacock.

  • Before Media Res, Ellenberg ran drama at HBO, overseeing Game of Thrones, Big Little Lies, True Detective and The Leftovers.

Palmer told TheWrap she self-produced because "the traditional doors of Hollywood were not necessarily opening for me in this genre," adding: "If I wanted to show people what I could do in comedy, I had to produce the content myself."
Why This Matters
Microdrama has entered the U.S. market mostly through platforms: Chinese-owned apps, studio experiments, publisher spinoffs. This is an established performer using it as her own casting demonstration, which is a different adoption path and a cheaper one, since the format needs no order and no partner to exist.

Palmer names the commercial case herself, calling out "the opportunity to launch and expand IP alongside promoting established properties within this space" and the appeal of a format that runs "without a long-term commitment."
Specific Implication
Talent with an owned character and no studio order can now build a produced showcase for it inside a format that requires no greenlight, and attach a platform to it afterward rather than before.
The Facts
  • The microseries rolled out on Audible and Palmer's social channels starting Monday August 17. Viewers see the character wake on her wedding day with several suitors who are not her husband.
  • Lady Miss Jacqueline originated in Palmer's 2016 digital sketch series "Southern Belle Insults."
  • Palmer on the format's fit: "Microdramas take what we love about over-the-top soap operas and deliver endless histrionic moments, and that is right up Lady Miss Jacqueline's alley!"
  • She performed standup in character on The Tonight Show earlier this summer, citing Flip Wilson as Geraldine and Ruth Buzzi as Gladys Ormphby as precedents, and calls herself "a throwback to the old vaudeville days."
  • Guests include Phaedra Parks, Zachariah Porter and Justin Sylvester.
  • Produced with Max Wyeth and Audible; directed by Kristen Brancaccio, who directed Hoorae's TikTok microdrama "Screen Time."

CEO Summary
The Motion Picture Association and ByteDance announced a memorandum of understanding establishing a framework to protect member studios' intellectual property across ByteDance's generative AI products. It covers the Seedance video generator and the Seedream image generator as delivered through TikTok, the TikTok USDS Joint Venture, CapCut and Dreamina. The agreement follows the MPA's February 2026 cease-and-desist letter over Seedance 2.0, and both sides cite the more recent Seedance 2.5 and Seedream 5.0 Pro releases as evidence of improved protections.

Charles Rivkin's statement describes the outcome as "meaningful guardrails," and guardrails are the entire consideration. Nothing in either company's announcement establishes a rate, a payment, or a licensing market for training material.

That is now the second time the MPA has reached this shape of settlement, after its criticism of OpenAI's Sora produced model-side filtering rather than compensation. The studios that want money rather than filters are pursuing it separately: Warner Bros., NBCUniversal and Disney are litigating against Midjourney on both training inputs and generated outputs, and that case is unaffected by this MOU.
Specific Implication
Rightsholders negotiating AI terms should not assume an industry-wide licensing rate is forming behind them. The trade body's two settlements to date have both produced filtering commitments, which means an individual rate has to be established deal by deal.

The bond amount is derived entirely from a term Paramount negotiated into its own merger agreement: $7 million per day owed to Warner Bros. Discovery shareholders starting September 30. That is the weakness the California attorney general's office attacked, arguing Paramount "stipulated to the timing it is now protesting" and did not request a bond when it agreed to hold off closing.

Judge Martinez-Olguin has already declined to require security once, waiving it in the July restraining order on the finding that "Plaintiff States bring suit to enforce important public interests." Acquirers structuring per-diem ticking fees into deals facing multi-state antitrust review should expect that cost to be treated as self-imposed rather than recoverable from challengers, and should negotiate the security question into the delay stipulation rather than after the trial date is set.

An AI microdrama series costs roughly $14,000 to $28,000 against over $100,000 for comparable live-action, and the production team can shrink from six people to one.
Why This Matters
Barmack's argument turns on where in the market substitution begins. The performer displaced here is Zhang Xiaolei, who made roughly 200 microdramas in two years and has had one booking in 2026, not a lead who commands a quote. The technology did not have to match a difficult performance to take that job; it had to clear the cheapest rung.

The licensing rates are the part that travels. ActID's $15 to $74 per episode is an observable price for a human face inside an AI production, and prices, once observable, get cited. Jeff Bridges described the same transaction from the other end of the market last week: "Pretty soon, I'll be out of a gig, man. I mean that. I'll probably lease my image." The distance between those two positions is the whole negotiation.
Specific Implication
Anyone drafting likeness terms for volume-tier performers should expect a counterparty to reach for a per-episode licensing figure rather than a session fee, and the reference points now in circulation are two figures under $100.
